D-Modules and Holonomic Functions

Anna-Laura Sattelberger and Bernd Sturmfels
Abstract

In algebraic geometry, one studies the solutions to polynomial equations, or, equivalently, to linear partial differential equations with constant coefficients. These lecture notes address the more general case when the coefficients are polynomials. The letter DD stands for the Weyl algebra, and a DD-module is a left module over DD. We focus on left ideals, or DD-ideals. We represent holonomic functions in several variables by the linear differential equations they satisfy. This encoding by a DD-ideal is useful for many problems, e.g., in geometry, physics and statistics. We explain how to work with holonomic functions. Applications include volume computations and likelihood inference.

Introduction

This article represents the notes for the three lectures delivered by the second author at the Math+ Fall School in Algebraic Geometry, held at FU Berlin from September 30 to October 4, 2019. The aim is to give an introduction to DD-modules and their use for concrete problems in applied algebraic geometry. This centers around the concept of a holonomic function in several variables. Such a function is among the solutions to a system of linear partial differential equations whose solution space is finite-dimensional. Our algebraic representation as a DD-ideal allows us to perform many operations with such objects.

The three lectures form the three sections of this article. In the first lecture, we introduce the basic tools. The focus is on computations that are built on Gröbner bases in the Weyl algebra. We review the Fundamental Theorem of Algebraic Analysis, we introduce holonomic DD-ideals, and we discuss their holonomic rank. Our presentation is based on the book [19].

In the second lecture, we study the problem of measuring areas and volumes of semi-algebraic sets. These quantities are naturally represented as integrals, and our task is to evaluate such an integral as accurately as is possible. To do so, we follow the approach of Lairez, Mezzarobba, and Safey El Din [15]. We introduce a parameter into the integrand, and we regard our integral as a function in that parameter. Such a volume function is holonomic, and we derive a DD-ideal that annihilates it. Using manipulations with that DD-ideal, we arrive at a scheme that allows for highly accurate numerical evaluation of the relevant integrals.

The third lecture is about connections to statistics. Many special functions arising in statistical inference are holonomic. We start out with likelihood functions for discrete models and their Bernstein–Sato polynomials, and we then discuss the holonomic gradient method and holonomic gradient descent. These were developed by a group of Japanese scholars [9, 17] for representing, evaluating and optimizing functions arising in statistics. We present an introduction to this theory, aiming to highlight many opportunities for further research. Our readers can hone their holonomic skills with a list of 1919 problems we provide at the end.

1 Tools

Our presentation follows closely that in [19, 26], albeit we use a slightly different notation. For any integer n≥1n\geq 1, we introduce the nnth Weyl algebra with complex coefficients:

D=ℂ[x1,…,xn]⟨∂1,…,∂n⟩.D\,\,=\,\,\mathbb{C}\left[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right]\langle\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}\rangle.

We sometimes write DnD_{n} instead of DD if we want to highlight the dimension nn of the ambient space. For the sake of brevity, we often write D=ℂ[x]⟨∂⟩D=\mathbb{C}[x]\langle\partial\rangle, especially when n=1n=1. Formally, DD is the free associative algebra over ℂ\mathbb{C} in the 2​n2n generators x1,…,xn,∂1,…,∂nx_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n} modulo the relations that all pairs of generators commute, with the exception of the nn special relations

∂ixi−xi∂i=  1fori=1,2,…,n.\hskip 10.00002pt\partial_{i}x_{i}-x_{i}\partial_{i}\,\,=\,\,1\hskip 20.00003pt\hbox{for}\,\,\,i=1,2,\ldots,n. (1)

The Weyl algebra DD is similar to a commutative polynomial ring in 2​n2n variables. But it is non-commutative, due to (1). A ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector space basis of DD consists of the normal monomials

xa∂b=x1a1x2a2⋯xnan∂1b1∂2b2⋯∂nbn.x^{a}\partial^{b}\hskip 10.00002pt=\hskip 10.00002ptx_{1}^{a_{1}}x_{2}^{a_{2}}\cdots x_{n}^{a_{n}}\partial_{1}^{b_{1}}\partial_{2}^{b_{2}}\cdots\partial_{n}^{b_{n}}.

Indeed, every word in the 2​n2n generators can be written uniquely as a ℤ\mathbb{Z}-linear combination of normal monomials. It is an instructive exercise to find this expansion for a monomial ∂uxv\partial^{u}x^{v}.

Many computer algebra systems have a built-in capability for computing in DD. For instance, in Macaulay2 [8], the expansion into normal monomials is done automatically.

Example 1.1.

Let n=2n=2, u=(2,3)u=(2,3) and v=(4,1)v=(4,1). The normal expansion of ∂uxv\partial^{u}x^{v} equals

∂12∂23x14x2=x14x2∂12∂23+3x14∂12∂22+8x13x2∂1∂23+24x13∂1∂22+12x12x2∂23+36x12∂22.\partial_{1}^{2}\partial_{2}^{3}x_{1}^{4}x_{2}\,\,=\,\,x_{1}^{4}x_{2}\partial_{1}^{2}\partial_{2}^{3}+3x_{1}^{4}\partial_{1}^{2}\partial_{2}^{2}+8x_{1}^{3}x_{2}\partial_{1}\partial_{2}^{3}+24x_{1}^{3}\partial_{1}\partial_{2}^{2}+12x_{1}^{2}x_{2}\partial_{2}^{3}+36x_{1}^{2}\partial_{2}^{2}. (2)

This can be found by hand. For this we recommend the following intermediate factorization:

(∂12x14)(∂23x2)=(x14∂12+8x13∂1+12x12)(x2∂23+3∂2).(\partial_{1}^{2}x_{1}^{4})(\partial_{2}^{3}x_{2})\,\,=\,\,\bigl(x_{1}^{4}\partial_{1}^{2}+8x_{1}^{3}\partial_{1}+12x_{1}^{2}\bigr)\bigl(x_{2}\partial_{2}^{3}+3\partial_{2}\bigr).

The formula (2) is the output when the following line is typed into Macaulay2 [8]:

D = QQ[x1,x2,d1,d2, WeylAlgebra => {x1=>d1,x2=>d2}];  d1^2*d2^3*x1^4*x2

Another important object is the ring of linear differential operators whose coefficients are rational functions in nn variables. We call this the rational Weyl algebra and we denote it by

R=ℂ(x1,…,xn)⟨∂1,…,∂n⟩orR=ℂ(x)⟨∂⟩.\,\,\,R\,\,=\,\,\mathbb{C}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\langle\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}\rangle\hskip 20.00003pt\text{or}\hskip 20.00003ptR\,=\,\mathbb{C}(x)\langle\partial\rangle.

Note that DD is a subalgebra of RR. The multiplication in RR is defined by the following rule:

∂ir(x)=r(x)∂i+∂r∂xi(x)for allr∈ℂ(x1,…,xn).\partial_{i}r(x)\,\,=\,\,r(x)\partial_{i}+\frac{\partial r}{\partial x_{i}}(x)\hskip 20.00003pt\hbox{for all}\,\,r\in\mathbb{C}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}). (3)

This simply extends the product rule (1) from polynomials to rational functions. The ring R1R_{1} is a (non-commutative) principal ideal domain, whereas D1D_{1} and R2R_{2} are not. But, a theorem due to Stafford [21] guarantees that every DD-ideal is generated by only two elements.

We are interested in studying left modules MM over the Weyl algebra DD or the rational Weyl algebra RR. Throughout these lecture notes, we denote the action of DD resp. RR on MM by

∙:D×M→M(resp. ∙:R×M→M).\bullet\colon D\times M\to M\hskip 10.00002pt\text{(resp. }\bullet\colon R\times M\to M\text{)}.

We are especially interested in left DD-modules of the form D/ID/I for some left ideal II in the Weyl algebra DD. Systems of linear partial differential equations with polynomial coefficients then can be investigated as modules over DD. Likewise, rational coefficients lead to modules over RR. Therefore, the theory of DD-modules allows us to study linear PDEs with polynomial coefficients by algebraic methods. In these notes we will exclusively deal with left modules over DD (resp. left ideals in DD) and will refer to them simply as DD-modules (resp. DD-ideals).

Remark 1.2.

In many sources, the theory of DD-modules is introduced more abstractly. Namely, one considers the sheaf 𝒟X\mathcal{D}_{X} of differential operators on some complex variety XX. Its sections on an affine open subset UU is the ring 𝒟X​(U)\mathcal{D}_{X}(U) of differential operators on the corresponding ℂ\mathbb{C}-algebra 𝒪X​(U)\mathcal{O}_{X}(U). In our case, X=𝔸ℂnX=\mathbb{A}_{\mathbb{C}}^{n} is affine nn-space over the complex numbers, so 𝒪X​(X)=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathcal{O}_{X}(X)=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] is the polynomial ring, and the Weyl algebra is recovered as the global sections of that sheaf. In symbols, we have D=𝒟X​(X)D=\mathcal{D}_{X}(X). Modules over DD then correspond precisely to 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}-quasi-coherent 𝒟X\mathcal{D}_{X}-modules, see [10, Proposition 1.4.4].

Example 1.3.

Many function spaces are DD-modules in a natural way. Let FF be a space of (infinitely differentiable) functions on a subset of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} that is closed under taking partial derivatives. The natural action of the Weyl algebra DD turns FF into a DD-module, as follows:

∙:D×F⟶F,(∂i,f)↦∂i∙f≔∂f∂xi,(xi,f)↦xi∙f≔xi⋅f.\bullet\colon D\times F\longrightarrow F,\hskip 10.00002pt(\partial_{i},f)\,\mapsto\,\partial_{i}\bullet f\,\coloneqq\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}},\hskip 10.00002pt(x_{i},f)\mapsto x_{i}\bullet f\,\coloneqq\,x_{i}\cdot f.
Definition 1.4.

We write Mod​(D)\text{Mod}(D) for the category of DD-modules. Let II be a DD-ideal and M∈Mod​(D)M\in\text{Mod}(D). The solution space of II in MM is the ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector space

SolM​(I)≔{m∈M∣P∙m=0​ for all ​P∈I}.\text{Sol}_{M}(I)\,\,\coloneqq\,\,\left\{m\in M\mid P\bullet m=0\text{ for all }P\in I\right\}.
Remark 1.5.

If P∈DP\in D and M∈Mod​(D)M\in\text{Mod}(D), then we have the vector space isomorphism

HomD​(D/D​P,M)≅{m∈M∣P∙m=0}.\text{Hom}_{D}\left(D/DP,M\right)\,\,\cong\,\,\left\{m\in M\mid P\bullet m=0\right\}.

This implies that SolM​(I){\rm Sol}_{M}(I) is isomorphic to HomD​(D/I,M)\text{Hom}_{D}\left(D/I,M\right).

In what follows, we will be relaxed about specifying the function space FF. The theory works best for holomorphic functions on a small open ball in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. For our applications in the later sections, we think of real-valued functions on an open subset of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, and we usually take DD with coefficients in ℚ\mathbb{Q}. We will often drop the subscript FF in SolF​(I){\rm Sol}_{F}(I) and assume that a suitable class FF of infinitely differentiable functions is understood from the context.

Example 1.6 (n=2n=2).

Let I=⟨∂1x1∂1,∂22+1⟩I=\langle\partial_{1}x_{1}\partial_{1},\partial_{2}^{2}+1\rangle. The solution space is four-dimensional:

Sol​(I)=ℂ⁡{sin⁡(x2),cos⁡(x2),log⁡(x1)​sin⁡(x2),log⁡(x1)​cos⁡(x2)}.\text{Sol}(I)\,\,=\,\,\mathbb{C}\bigl\{\,\sin(x_{2}),\,\cos(x_{2}),\,\log(x_{1})\sin(x_{2}),\,\log(x_{1})\cos(x_{2})\bigr\}.

The reader is urged to verify this and to experiment. What happens if ∂22+1\partial_{2}^{2}+1 is replaced by ∂23+1\partial_{2}^{3}+1? What if ∂1x1∂1\partial_{1}x_{1}\partial_{1} is replaced by ∂1x1∂1x1∂1\partial_{1}x_{1}\partial_{1}x_{1}\partial_{1}, or if some indices 11 are turned into 22?

The Weyl algebra DD has three important subrings that are commutative polynomial rings:

  • •

    The usual polynomial ring ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] acts by multiplication. Its ideals represent subvarieties of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. In analysis, this models distributions supported on subvarieties.

  • •

    The ring ℂ[∂1,…,∂n]\mathbb{C}[\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}] of linear partial differential operators with constant coefficients. Solving such PDEs is very interesting already. This was highlighted in [23, Chapter 10].

  • •

    The ring ℂ⁡[θ1,…,θn]\mathbb{C}[\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n}], where θi≔xi∂i\theta_{i}\coloneqq x_{i}\partial_{i}. The sum θ1+⋯+θn\theta_{1}+\cdots+\theta_{n} is known as the Euler operator. The joint eigenvectors of the operators θ1,…,θn\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n} are precisely the monomials.

Example 1.7 (n=1n=1).

Replacing the derivatives ∂i\partial_{i} by the θi\theta_{i} has an interesting effect on the solutions. It replaces each coordinate xix_{i} by log⁡(xi){\rm log}(x_{i}). In one variable, we suppress the indices:

  • •

    Let I=⟨(∂+3)2(∂−7)⟩I=\langle(\partial+3)^{2}(\partial-7)\rangle. Then Sol⁡(I)=ℂ⁡{exp⁡(−3​x),x​exp⁡(−3​x),exp⁡(7​x)}\Sol(I)=\mathbb{C}\left\{\exp(-3x),x\exp(-3x),\exp(7x)\right\}.

  • •

    Let J=⟨(θ+3)2​(θ−7)⟩J=\langle(\theta+3)^{2}(\theta-7)\rangle. Then Sol⁡(J)=ℂ⁡{x−3,log⁡(x)​x−3,x7}\Sol(J)=\mathbb{C}\left\{x^{-3},\log(x)x^{-3},x^{7}\right\}.

The reader is encouraged to try the same for their favorite polynomial ideal in nn variables.

Every PP in the Weyl algebra DD has a unique expansion into normally ordered monomials,

P=∑(a,b)∈Eca​bxa∂b,P\,\,=\sum_{(a,b)\in E}c_{ab}x^{a}\partial^{b},

where ca​b∈ℂ\{0}c_{ab}\in\mathbb{C}\backslash\{0\} and EE is a finite subset of ℕ2​n\mathbb{N}^{2n}. Fix u,v∈ℝnu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with u+v≥0u+v\geq 0 and set m=max(a,b)∈E⁡(a⋅u+b⋅v)m=\max_{(a,b)\in E}\left(a\cdot u+b\cdot v\right). The initial form of P∈D\,P\in D\, is defined to be

in(u,v)(P)=∑a⋅u+b⋅v=mca​b∏uk+vk>0xkakξkbk∏uk+vk=0xkak∂kbk∈gr(u,v)(D).\ini_{(u,v)}(P)\hskip 10.00002pt=\sum_{a\cdot u+b\cdot v=m}\!\!c_{ab}\prod_{u_{k}+v_{k}>0}\!\!x_{k}^{a_{k}}\xi_{k}^{b_{k}}\prod_{u_{k}+v_{k}=0}\!\!x_{k}^{a_{k}}\partial_{k}^{b_{k}}\,\,\,\in\,\,\,\text{gr}_{(u,v)}\left(D\right).

Here ξk\xi_{k} is a new formal variable that commutes with all other variables. The initial form is an element in the associated graded ring under the filtration of DD given by the weights (u,v)(u,v):

gr(u,v)​(D)={D if ​u+v=0,ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn,ξ1,…,ξn] if ​u+v>0,a mixture of the above otherwise.\text{gr}_{(u,v)}(D)\,\,=\,\,\begin{cases}D&\text{ if }u+v=0,\\ \mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n}]&\text{ if }u+v>0,\\ \text{a mixture of the above}&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

A particular interest is the case when uu is the zero vector and vv is the all-one vector e=(1,1,…,1)e=(1,1,\ldots,1). Analysts refer to in(0,e)​(P){\rm in}_{(0,e)}(P) as the symbol of the differential operator PP. Thus, the symbol of a differential operator in DD is simply an ordinary polynomial in 2​n2n variables.

We continue to allow arbitrary weights u,v∈ℝnu,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n} that satisfy u+v≥0u+v\geq 0. For a DD-ideal II, the vector space in(u,v)⁡(I)=ℂ⁡{in(u,v)⁡(P)∣P∈I}\ini_{(u,v)}(I)=\mathbb{C}\left\{\ini_{(u,v)}(P)\mid P\in I\right\} is a left ideal in gr(u,v)​(D)\text{gr}_{(u,v)}(D). The computation of the initial ideals in(u,v)⁡(I)\ini_{(u,v)}(I) and their associated Gröbner bases via the Buchberger algorithm in DD is the engine behind many practical applications of DD-modules.

Definition 1.8.

Fix e=(1,1,…,1)e=(1,1,\ldots,1) and 0=(0,0,…,0)0=(0,0,\ldots,0) in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Given any DD-ideal II, the characteristic variety Char⁡(I)\charv(I) is the affine variety in ℂ2​n\mathbb{C}^{2n} that is defined by the characteristic ideal ch⁡(I)≔in(0,e)⁡(I)\,\ch(I)\coloneqq\ini_{(0,e)}(I). This is the ideal in ℂ⁡[x,ξ]=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn,ξ1,…,ξn]\mathbb{C}[x,\xi]=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n}] which is generated by the symbols in(0,e)​(P){\rm in}_{(0,e)}(P) of all differential operators P∈IP\in I. In the theory of DD-modules, one refers to Char⁡(I)\charv(I) as the characteristic variety of the DD-module D/ID/I.

Example 1.9 (n=2n=2).

Let I=⟨x1∂2,x2∂1⟩I=\langle x_{1}\partial_{2},x_{2}\partial_{1}\rangle. The two generators are not a Gröbner basis of II. To get a Gröbner basis, one also needs their commutator. The characteristic ideal is

ch⁡(I)=⟨x1​ξ2,x2​ξ1,x1​ξ1−x2​ξ2⟩=⟨x1,x2⟩∩⟨ξ1,ξ2⟩∩⟨x12,x22,x1​ξ2,x2​ξ1,ξ12,ξ22,x1​ξ1−x2​ξ2⟩.\ch(I)=\langle x_{1}\xi_{2},x_{2}\xi_{1},x_{1}\xi_{1}-x_{2}\xi_{2}\rangle=\langle x_{1},x_{2}\rangle\,\cap\,\langle\xi_{1},\xi_{2}\rangle\,\cap\,\langle x_{1}^{2},x_{2}^{2},x_{1}\xi_{2},x_{2}\xi_{1},\xi_{1}^{2},\xi_{2}^{2},x_{1}\xi_{1}-x_{2}\xi_{2}\rangle.

The last ideal is primary to the embedded prime ⟨x1,x2,ξ1,ξ2⟩\langle x_{1},x_{2},\xi_{1},\xi_{2}\rangle. The characteristic variety is the union of two planes, defined by the two minimal primes, that meet in the origin in ℂ4\mathbb{C}^{4}.

Theorem 1.10 (Fundamental Theorem of Algebraic Analysis).

Let II be a proper DD-ideal. Every irreducible component of its characteristic variety Char⁡(I)\charv(I) has dimension at least nn.

This theorem was established by M. Sato, T. Kawai, and M. Kashiwara in [20].

Definition 1.11.

A DD-ideal II is called holonomic if dim(Char⁡(I))=n\dim\left(\charv(I)\right)=n, i.e., if the dimension of its characteristic variety in ℂ2​n\mathbb{C}^{2n} is as small as possible. We fix the field ℂ⁡(x)=ℂ⁡(x1,…,xn)\,\mathbb{C}(x)=\mathbb{C}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\, and the polynomial ring ℂ⁡(x)​[ξ]=ℂ⁡(x)​[ξ1,…,ξn]\,\mathbb{C}(x)[\xi]=\mathbb{C}(x)[\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n}]\, over that field. The holonomic rank of a DD-ideal II is rank⁡(I)=dimℂ⁡(x)(ℂ⁡(x)​[ξ]/ℂ⁡(x)​[ξ]​ch⁡(I))=dimℂ⁡(x)(R/R​I)\,\rank(I)\,=\,\dim_{\mathbb{C}(x)}\bigl(\mathbb{C}(x)[\xi]/\mathbb{C}(x)[\xi]\ch(I)\bigr)\,=\,\dim_{\mathbb{C}(x)}\left(R/RI\right). Both dimensions are given by the number of standard monomials for a Gröbner basis of II in RR with respect to ee. The ideal in Example 1.9 is holonomic and its holonomic rank is 11.

If a DD-ideal II is holonomic, then rank⁡(I)<∞\rank(I)<\infty. But, the converse is not true. For instance, consider the DD-ideal I=⟨x1∂12,x1∂23⟩I=\langle x_{1}\partial_{1}^{2},x_{1}\partial_{2}^{3}\rangle. Its characteristic ideal equals ch⁡(I)=⟨x1⟩∩⟨ξ12,ξ23⟩{\rm ch}(I)=\langle x_{1}\rangle\cap\langle\xi_{1}^{2},\xi_{2}^{3}\rangle, so Char⁡(I)\charv(I) has dimension 33 in ℂ4\mathbb{C}^{4}, which means that II is not holonomic. After passing to rational function coefficients, we have ℂ⁡(x)​[ξ]​ch​(I)=⟨ξ12,ξ23⟩\mathbb{C}(x)[\xi]{\rm ch}(I)=\langle\xi_{1}^{2},\xi_{2}^{3}\rangle, and hence rank⁡(I)=6<∞{\rm rank}(I)=6<\infty.

We define the Weyl closure of a DD-ideal II to be the DD-ideal W⁡(I)≔R​I∩DW(I)\coloneqq RI\cap D. We always have I⊆W⁡(I)I\subseteq W(I), and II is Weyl-closed if I=W⁡(I)I=W(I) holds. The operation of passing to the Weyl closure is analogous to that of passing to the radical in a polynomial ring. Namely, W⁡(I)W(I) is the ideal of all differential operators that annihilate all classical solutions of II. In particular, it fulfills rank⁡(I)=rank⁡(W⁡(I)){\rm rank}(I)={\rm rank}(W(I)). If I=⟨x1∂12,x1∂23⟩I=\langle x_{1}\partial_{1}^{2},x_{1}\partial_{2}^{3}\rangle then W(I)=⟨∂12,∂23⟩W(I)=\langle\partial_{1}^{2},\partial_{2}^{3}\rangle, and

Sol⁡(I)=Sol⁡(W⁡(I))=ℂ⁡{1,x1,x2,x1​x2,x22,x1​x22}.{\rm Sol}(I)\,=\,{\rm Sol}(W(I))\,=\,\mathbb{C}\{1,x_{1},x_{2},x_{1}x_{2},x_{2}^{2},x_{1}x_{2}^{2}\}.

In general, it is a difficult task to compute the Weyl closure W⁡(I)W(I) from given generators of II.

Definition 1.12.

The singular locus Sing⁡(I)\Sing(I) of II is the variety in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} defined by the ideal

sing⁡(I)≔(ch⁡(I):⟨ξ1,…,ξn⟩∞)∩ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn].\sing(I)\,\,\coloneqq\,\,\bigl(\ch(I):\langle\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n}\rangle^{\infty}\bigr)\,\cap\,\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]. (4)

Geometrically, the singular locus is the closure of the projection of Char⁡(I)\(ℂn×{0})\,\charv(I)\backslash(\mathbb{C}^{n}\times\{0\})\, onto the first nn coordinates of ℂ2​n\mathbb{C}^{2n}. If II is holonomic, then Sing⁡(I)\Sing(I) is a proper subvariety of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. For instance, in Example 1.7 with n=1n=1, we have Sing⁡(I)=∅{\rm Sing}(I)=\emptyset whereas Sing⁡(J)={0}{\rm Sing}(J)=\{0\} in ℂ1\mathbb{C}^{1}.

Example 1.13 (n=4n=4).

Fix constants a,b,c∈ℂa,b,c\in\mathbb{C} and consider the DD-ideal

I=⟨θ1−θ4+1−c,θ2+θ4+a,θ3+θ4+b,∂2∂3−∂1∂4⟩.I\,\,=\,\,\langle\,\,\theta_{1}-\theta_{4}+1-c,\,\theta_{2}+\theta_{4}+a,\,\theta_{3}+\theta_{4}+b\,,\,\partial_{2}\partial_{3}-\partial_{1}\partial_{4}\rangle. (5)

The first three operators tell us that every solution g∈Sol⁡(I)g\in{\rm Sol}(I) is ℤ3\mathbb{Z}^{3}-homogeneous, as follows:

g⁡(x)=x1c−1​x2−a​x3−b⋅f⁡(x1​x4x2​x3)for some function f.g(x)\,=\,x_{1}^{c-1}x_{2}^{-a}x_{3}^{-b}\cdot f\bigl(\frac{x_{1}x_{4}}{x_{2}x_{3}}\bigr)\hskip 20.00003pt\hbox{for some function $f$.}

The last generator of the DD-ideal II implies that the univariate function ff satisfies

x⁡(1−x)​f′′+(c−x⁡(a+b+1))​f′−a​b​f=0.x(1-x)f^{\prime\prime}+(c-x(a+b+1))f^{\prime}-abf=0.

This second-order ODE is Gauß’ hypergeometric equation. The DD-ideal II is the Gel’fand–Kapranov–Zelevinsky (GKZ) representation of Gauß’ hypergeometric function. We have

ch⁡(I)=⟨ξ2​ξ3−ξ1​ξ4,x1​ξ1−x4​ξ4,x2​ξ2+x4​ξ4,x3​ξ3+x4​ξ4⟩.\ch(I)\,\,=\,\,\langle\xi_{2}\xi_{3}-\xi_{1}\xi_{4},x_{1}\xi_{1}-x_{4}\xi_{4},x_{2}\xi_{2}+x_{4}\xi_{4},x_{3}\xi_{3}+x_{4}\xi_{4}\rangle.

This characteristic ideal has ten associated primes, one for each face of a square. Using the ideal operations in (4) we find that sing⁡(I)=⟨x1​x2​x3​x4​(x1​x4−x2​x3)⟩\sing(I)=\langle\,x_{1}x_{2}x_{3}x_{4}(x_{1}x_{4}-x_{2}x_{3})\,\rangle. The generator is the principal determinant of the matrix (x1x2x3x4)\begin{pmatrix}x_{1}&x_{2}\\ x_{3}&x_{4}\end{pmatrix}, i.e., the product of all of its subdeterminants.

Theorem 1.14 (Cauchy–Kowalevskii–Kashiwara).

Let II be a holonomic DD-ideal and let U\,U be an open subset of ℂn\Sing⁡(I)\mathbb{C}^{n}\backslash\Sing(I) that is simply connected. Then the space of holomorphic solutions to II on UU has dimension equal to rank⁡(I)\rank(I). In symbols, dim⁡(Sol⁡(I))=rank⁡(I){\rm dim}({\rm Sol}(I))=\rank(I).

For a discussion of this theorem and pointers to proofs, we refer to [19, Theorem 1.4.19].

Example 1.15.

The DD-ideal II in (5) is holonomic with rank⁡(I)=2{\rm rank}(I)=2. Outside the singular locus in ℂ4\mathbb{C}^{4}, it has two independent solutions. These arise from Gauß’ hypergeometric ODE.

This raises the question of how one can compute a basis for Sol⁡(I){\rm Sol}(I) when II is holonomic. To answer this question, let us think about the case n=1n=1. Here, the classical Frobenius method can be used to construct a basis consisting of series solutions. These have the form

p⁡(x)=xa​log​(x)b+higher order terms.p(x)\hskip 10.00002pt=\hskip 10.00002ptx^{a}{\rm log}(x)^{b}\,+\,\hbox{higher order terms}. (6)

The exponent aa is a complex number. It is a zero of the indicial polynomial of the given ODE. Here the multiplicity of this zero is <b<b. In particular, bb is a nonnegative integer.

The following example is taken from the Wikipedia entry for “Frobenius method”.

Example 1.16.

We are looking for a solution pp to the equation x2​p′′−x​p′+(1−x)​p=0\,x^{2}p^{\prime\prime}-xp^{\prime}+(1-x)p=0. This equation is equivalent to pp being a solution of I=⟨θ2−2​θ+1−x⟩\,I=\langle\theta^{2}-2\theta+1-x\rangle. The indicial polynomial is the generator of the initial ideal in(−1,1)​(I)=⟨(θ−1)2⟩{\rm in}_{(-1,1)}(I)=\langle\,(\theta-1)^{2}\,\rangle. The solution basis consists of two series (6) with a=1a=1 and b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}. The higher order terms of these series are computed by solving the linear recurrences for the coefficients that are induced by II.

Let now n≥1n\geq 1 be any positive integer. The algebraic nn-torus T≔(ℂ\{0})nT\coloneqq(\mathbb{C}\backslash\{0\})^{n} acts naturally on the Weyl algebra DD, by scaling the generators ∂i\partial_{i} and xix_{i} in a reciprocal manner:

∘:T×D⟶D,(t,∂i)↦ti∂i,(t,xi)↦1tixi.\circ\,\colon T\times D\longrightarrow D,\hskip 10.00002pt(t,\partial_{i})\mapsto t_{i}\partial_{i},\ (t,x_{i})\mapsto\frac{1}{t_{i}}x_{i}.

This action is well-defined because it preserves the defining relations (1). A DD-ideal II is said to be torus-fixed if t∘I=It\circ I=I for all t∈Tt\in T. Torus-fixed DD-ideals play the role of monomial ideals in an ordinary commutative polynomial ring. They can be described as follows:

Proposition 1.17.

The following three conditions are equivalent for a DD-ideal II:

  • (a)

    II is torus-fixed,

  • (b)

    I=in(−w,w)⁡(I)I=\ini_{(-w,w)}(I) for all w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

  • (c)

    II is generated by operators of the form xap(θ)∂bx^{a}p(\theta)\partial^{b} where a,b∈ℕna,b\in\mathbb{N}^{n} and p∈ℂ⁡[θ]p\in\mathbb{C}[\theta].

Just like in the commutative case, initial ideals with respect to generic weights are torus-fixed. Namely, given any DD-ideal II, if ww is generic in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, then in(−w,w)⁡(I)\ini_{(-w,w)}(I) is torus-fixed. Note that in(−w,w)⁡(I)\ini_{(-w,w)}(I) is also a DD-ideal, and it is important to understand how its solution space is related to that of II. Lifting the former to the latter is the key to the Frobenius method.

Let w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and suppose that ff is a holomorphic function on an appropriate subset of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. We assume that a series expansion of ff has the lowest order form inw⁡(f)\ini_{w}(f), called initial series with respect to assigning the weight wiw_{i} for the coordinate xix_{i} for all ii (see [19, Definition 2.5.4] for details). Under this assumption, the following holds:

Proposition 1.18.

If f∈Sol⁡(I)\,f\in\Sol(I)\, then inw⁡(f)∈Sol⁡(in(−w,w)⁡(I))\,\ini_{w}(f)\in\Sol\bigl(\ini_{(-w,w)}(I)\bigr).

This fact is reminiscent of the use of tropical geometry [16] in solving polynomial equations. The tropical limit of an ideal in a (Laurent) polynomial ring is given by a monomial-free initial ideal. The zeros of the latter furnish the starting terms in a series solution of the former, where each series is a scalar in a field like the Puiseux series or the pp-adic numbers.

We now focus on the polynomial subring ℂ⁡[θ]=ℂ⁡[θ1,…,θn]\mathbb{C}[\theta]=\mathbb{C}[\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n}] in the Weyl algebra DD.

Definition 1.19.

The distraction of a DD-ideal II is the polynomial ideal I~≔R​I∩ℂ⁡[θ]\,\widetilde{I}\coloneqq RI\cap\mathbb{C}[\theta].

By definition, I~\widetilde{I} is contained in the Weyl closure W⁡(I)W(I). If II is torus-fixed, then II and I~\widetilde{I} have the same Weyl closure, W⁡(I)=W⁡(I~)W(I)=W(\widetilde{I}), by Proposition 1.17. This means that the classical solutions to II are represented by an ideal in the commutative polynomial ring ℂ⁡[θ]\mathbb{C}[\theta].

Theorem 1.20.

Let II be a torus-fixed ideal, with generators xap(θ)∂b\,x^{a}p(\theta)\partial^{b}\, for various a,b∈ℕna,b\in\mathbb{N}^{n}. The distraction I~\widetilde{I} is generated by the corresponding polynomials [θ]b⋅p⁡(θ−b)\,[\theta]_{b}\cdot p(\theta-b), where

[θ]b=∏i=1n∏j=0bi−1(θi−j)[\theta]_{b}\,=\,\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=0}^{b_{i}-1}(\theta_{i}-j)

denotes falling factorials.

It is instructive to study the case when II is generated by an Artinian monomial ideal in ℂ[∂]\mathbb{C}[\partial]. In this case, I~\widetilde{I} is the radical ideal whose zeros are the points under the staircase of II.

Example 1.21 (n=2n=2).

Let I=⟨∂13,∂1∂2,∂22⟩I=\langle\partial_{1}^{3},\partial_{1}\partial_{2},\partial_{2}^{2}\rangle. The points under the staircase of II are (0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(0,1)(0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(0,1). The distraction is the radical ideal

I~=⟨θ1​(θ1−1)​(θ1−2),θ1​θ2,θ2​(θ2−1)⟩=⟨θ1,θ2⟩∩⟨θ1−1,θ2⟩∩⟨θ1−2,θ2⟩∩⟨θ1,θ2−1⟩.\begin{matrix}\widetilde{I}&=&\bigl\langle\,\theta_{1}(\theta_{1}-1)(\theta_{1}-2)\,,\,\theta_{1}\theta_{2}\,,\,\theta_{2}(\theta_{2}-1)\,\bigr\rangle\qquad\qquad\\ &=&\langle\theta_{1},\theta_{2}\rangle\,\cap\,\langle\theta_{1}-1,\theta_{2}\rangle\,\cap\,\langle\theta_{1}-2,\theta_{2}\rangle\,\cap\,\langle\theta_{1},\theta_{2}-1\rangle.\end{matrix}

The solutions are spanned by the standard monomials: Sol⁡(I)=Sol⁡(I~)=ℂ⁡{1,x1,x12,x2}\,\Sol(I)=\Sol(\widetilde{I})=\mathbb{C}\left\{1,x_{1},x_{1}^{2},x_{2}\right\}.

A Frobenius ideal is a DD-ideal that is generated by elements of ℂ⁡[θ]\mathbb{C}[\theta]. Thus, every torus-fixed ideal II gives rise to a Frobenius ideal D​I~D\widetilde{I} that has the same classical solution space. The solution space can be described explicitly when the given ideal in ℂ⁡[θ]\mathbb{C}[\theta] is Artinian.

Let JJ be an Artinian ideal in the polynomial ring ℂ⁡[θ]=ℂ⁡[θ1,…,θn]\mathbb{C}[\theta]=\mathbb{C}[\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n}]. Then its variety V⁡(J)V(J) is a finite subset of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. The primary decomposition of JJ looks like

J=⋂u∈V⁡(J)Qu​(θ−u),J=\bigcap_{u\in V(J)}Q_{u}(\theta-u),

where QuQ_{u} is an ideal that is primary to the maximal ideal ⟨θ1,…,θn⟩\langle\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n}\rangle and Qu​(θ−u)Q_{u}(\theta-u) is the ideal obtained from QuQ_{u} by replacing θi\theta_{i} with θi−ui\theta_{i}-u_{i} for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n. We call QuQ_{u} the primary component of JJ at uu. Its orthogonal complement is the finite-dimensional vector space

Qu⟂≔{g∈ℂ[x1,…,xn]∣f(∂1,…,∂n)∙g(x1,…,xn)=0 for all f=f(θ1,…,θn)∈Qu}.\displaystyle Q_{u}^{\perp}\coloneqq\left\{g\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]\mid f(\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n})\bullet g(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0\text{ for all }f=f(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n})\in Q_{u}\right\}.

In commutative algebra, the space Qu⟂Q_{u}^{\perp} is known as the inverse system to JJ at uu. Note that Qu⟂Q_{u}^{\perp} is a module over ℂ[∂]=ℂ[∂1,…,∂n]\mathbb{C}[\partial]=\mathbb{C}[\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}]. If this module is cyclic, then JJ is Gorenstein at uu. The ℂ\mathbb{C}-dimension of Qu⟂Q_{u}^{\perp} is the multiplicity of the point uu as a zero of the ideal JJ.

Theorem 1.22.

Given an ideal JJ in the polynomial ring ℂ⁡[θ]\mathbb{C}[\theta], the corresponding Frobenius ideal I=D​JI=DJ in the Weyl algebra DD is holonomic if and only if JJ is Artinian. In this case, rank⁡(I)=dimℂ​(ℂ⁡[θ]/J)\,\rank(I)={\rm dim}_{\mathbb{C}}\bigl(\mathbb{C}[\theta]/J\bigr), and the solution space Sol⁡(I)\,{\rm Sol}(I) is spanned by the functions

x1u1⋯xnun⋅g(log(x1),…,log(xn)),x_{1}^{u_{1}}\cdots x_{n}^{u_{n}}\cdot g({\rm log}(x_{1}),\ldots,{\rm log}(x_{n})),

where u∈V⁡(J)u\in V(J) and g∈Qu⟂g\in Q_{u}^{\perp} runs over all polynomials in the inverse system to JJ at uu.

The theorem implies that the space of logarithmic solutions gg is given by the primary component at the origin. Hence, it is interesting to study ideals that are primary to ⟨θ1,…,θn⟩\langle\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n}\rangle.

Example 1.23 (n=3n=3).

The ideal J=⟨θ1+θ2+θ3,θ1​θ2+θ1​θ3+θ2​θ3,θ1​θ2​θ3⟩\,J=\langle\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}+\theta_{3},\theta_{1}\theta_{2}+\theta_{1}\theta_{3}+\theta_{2}\theta_{3},\theta_{1}\theta_{2}\theta_{3}\rangle\, is generated by non-constant symmetric polynomials. It is primary to ⟨θ1,θ2,θ3⟩\langle\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3}\rangle. We have 𝒱⁡(J)={(0,0,0)}\mathcal{V}(J)=\{(0,0,0)\}, with rank⁡(J)=6\rank(J)=6. The inverse system is the 66-dimensional space spanned by all polynomials that are successive partial derivatives of (x1−x2)​(x1−x3)​(x2−x3)(x_{1}-x_{2})(x_{1}-x_{3})(x_{2}-x_{3}). This implies

Sol⁡(J)=ℂ⁡[θ]∙(log⁡(x1x2)​log⁡(x1x3)​log⁡(x2x3))≅ℂ6.\Sol(J)\,\,=\,\,\mathbb{C}[\theta]\bullet\left(\log\left(\frac{x_{1}}{x_{2}}\right)\log\left(\frac{x_{1}}{x_{3}}\right)\log\left(\frac{x_{2}}{x_{3}}\right)\right)\,\,\,\cong\,\,\,\mathbb{C}^{6}.

Gorenstein ideals like JJ are ubiquitous in the application of DD-modules to mirror symmetry.

The term “Frobenius ideal” is a reference to the Frobenius method, which we now extend from ODEs to PDEs. The role of the indicial polynomial is now played by the indicial ideal.

Theorem 1.24.

Let II be any holonomic DD-ideal and w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n} generic. The indicial ideal

indw⁡(I)≔in(−w,w)⁡(I)~\ind_{w}(I)\,\,\coloneqq\,\,\widetilde{\ini_{(-w,w)}(I)}

is a holonomic Frobenius ideal, whose rank is equal to the rank of in(−w,w)⁡(I)\,\ini_{(-w,w)}(I). This rank is bounded above by rank⁡(I)\rank(I), with equality when the DD-ideal II is regular holonomic.

We refer to [19, Section 2.4] for the definition of regular holonomic and [19, Theorem 2.5.1] for this result. The indicial ideal indw⁡(I)\ind_{w}(I) is computed from II with Gröbner bases in DD. This computation identifies the leading terms in a basis of regular series solutions for II.

Example 1.25 (n=1n=1).

We illustrate Theorem 1.24 for the ODE in Example 1.16. Let I=⟨x2∂2−x∂+1−x⟩I=\langle x^{2}\partial^{2}-x\partial+1-x\rangle and set w=1w=1. The indicial ideal indw​(I)\,{\rm ind}_{w}(I)\, is the principal ideal in ℂ⁡[θ]\mathbb{C}[\theta] generated by θ2−2​θ+1\theta^{2}-2\theta+1. This polynomial has the unique root u=1u=1 with multiplicity 22. Hence, we obtain a basis of series solutions to II which take the form x+⋯x+\cdots and x⋅log⁡(x)+⋯x\cdot{\rm log}(x)+\cdots.

2 Volumes

In calculus, we learn about definite integrals in order to determine the area under a graph. Likewise, in multivariable calculus, we examine the volume enclosed by a surface. We are here interested in areas and volumes of semi-algebraic sets. When these sets depend on one or more parameters, their volumes are holonomic functions of the parameters. We explain what this means and how it can be used for highly accurate evaluation of volume functions.

Suppose that MM is a DD-module. We say that MM is torsion-free if it is torsion-free as a module over the polynomial ring ℂ⁡[x]=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{C}[x]=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]. In our applications, MM is usually a space of infinitely differentiable functions on a simply connected open set in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} or ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. Such DD-modules are always torsion-free. For a function f∈Mf\in M, its annihilator is the DD-ideal

AnnD​(f)≔{P∈D∣P∙f=0}.\text{Ann}_{D}\left(f\right)\,\,\coloneqq\,\left\{\,P\in D\mid P\bullet f=0\,\right\}.

In general, it is a non-trivial task to compute the annihilating ideal. But, in some cases, computer algebra systems can help us to compute holonomic annihilating ideals. For rational functions r∈ℚ⁡(x)r\in\mathbb{Q}(x) this can be done in Macaulay2 with a built-in command as follows:

needsPackage "Dmodules"; D = QQ[x1,x2,d1,d2, WeylAlgebra => {x1=>d1,x2=>d2}];
rnum = x1;  rden = x2;   I = RatAnn(rnum,rden)

Users of Singular can do the same with the library dmodapp_lib [3]:

LIB "dmodapp.lib";
ring s=0,(x1,x2),dp; setring s;
poly rnum=x1; poly rden=x2;
def an=annRat(rnum,rden); setring an;
LD;

Do try this with your own choice of numerator rnum and denominator rden. These should be polynomials in x1 and x2. In our example we learn that r=x1/x2r=x_{1}/x_{2} has the annihilator

AnnD(r)=⟨∂12,x1∂1−1,(x2∂2+1)∂1⟩.{\rm Ann}_{D}(r)\hskip 10.00002pt=\hskip 10.00002pt\langle\,\partial_{1}^{2},\,x_{1}\partial_{1}-1,\,(x_{2}\partial_{2}+1)\partial_{1}\,\rangle.

Suppose now that f⁡(x1,…,xn)f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) is an algebraic function. This means that ff satisfies some polynomial equation F⁡(f,x1,…,xn)=0F(f,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=0. Using the polynomial FF as its input, the Mathematica package HolonomicFunctions can compute a holonomic representation of ff. The output is a linear differential operator of lowest degree annihilating ff. See Example 2.4.

Let MM be DD-module and f∈Mf\in M. We say that ff is holonomic if AnnD​(f){\rm Ann}_{D}(f) is a holonomic DD-ideal. If ff is a function on a subset of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} or ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}, we refer to it as a holonomic function.

Proposition 2.1.

Let ff be an element in a torsion-free DD-module MM. Then the following three conditions are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    ff is holonomic,

  2. (b)

    rank​(AnnD​(f))<∞\text{rank}\left(\text{Ann}_{D}(f)\right)<\infty,

  3. (c)

    for each i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\} there is an operator Pi∈ℂ[x1,…,xn]⟨∂i⟩\{0}P_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]\langle\partial_{i}\rangle\backslash\{0\} that annihilates ff.

Proof.

Let I=AnnD⁡(f)I=\ann_{D}(f). If II is holonomic, then R​IRI is a zero-dimensional ideal in RR. This condition is equivalent to (b) and (c). For the implication from (b) to (a) we note that AnnD⁡(f)\ann_{D}(f) is Weyl-closed, since MM is torsion-free. Finally, since by assumption rank​(AnnD​(f))<∞\text{rank}\left(\text{Ann}_{D}(f)\right)<\infty, AnnD⁡(f)=W⁡(AnnD⁡(f))\ann_{D}(f)=W(\ann_{D}(f)) is holonomic by [19, Theorem 1.4.15]. ∎

Remark 2.2.

Let I=AnnD​(f)I={\rm Ann}_{D}(f) be the annihilator of a holonomic function ff, and fix a point x0∈ℂnx_{0}\in\mathbb{C}^{n} that is not in the singular locus of II. Let m1,…,mnm_{1},\ldots,m_{n} be the orders of the distinguished operators P1,…,Pn∈IP_{1},\ldots,P_{n}\in I in Proposition 2.1 (c). Thus, PkP_{k} is a differential operator in ∂k\partial_{k} of order mkm_{k} whose coefficients are polynomials in x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}. Suppose we impose initial conditions by specifying complex numbers for the m1m2⋯mnm_{1}m_{2}\cdots m_{n} quantities

(∂1i1⋯∂nin∙f)∣x=x0where   0≤ik<mk for k=1,…,n.(\partial_{1}^{i_{1}}\cdots\partial_{n}^{i_{n}}\bullet f)\!\!\mid_{x=x_{0}}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{where}\,\,\,0\leq i_{k}<m_{k}\,\text{ for }\,k=1,\ldots,n. (7)

The operators P1,…,PnP_{1},\ldots,P_{n} together with the initial conditions (7) specify the function ff uniquely inside Sol⁡(I){\rm Sol}(I). This is known as canonical holonomic representation [28, Section 4.1].

Many interesting functions are holonomic. To begin with, every rational function rr in x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n} is holonomic. This follows from Proposition 2.1 (c), since rr is annihilated by

r(x)∂i−∂r∂xi∈Rfori=1,2,…,n.r(x)\partial_{i}\,-\,\frac{\partial r}{\partial x_{i}}\,\in\,R\hskip 20.00003pt\hbox{for}\,\,\,\,i=1,2,\ldots,n. (8)

By clearing denominators in this first-order operator, we obtain a non-zero Pi∈ℂ[x]⟨∂i⟩P_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[x]\langle\partial_{i}\rangle with mi=1m_{i}=1 that annihilates rr. These operators, together with fixing the value r⁡(x0)r(x_{0}) at a general point x0∈ℂnx_{0}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}, constitute a canonical holonomic representation. If r⁡(x)r(x) is rational, then the function g⁡(x)=exp⁡(r⁡(x))g(x)={\rm exp}(r(x)) is also holonomic. The role of (8) is now played by

∂i−∂r∂xi∈Rfori=1,2,…,n.\partial_{i}\,-\,\frac{\partial r}{\partial x_{i}}\,\in\,R\hskip 20.00003pt\hbox{for}\,\,i=1,2,\ldots,n. (9)

By the Chain Rule, these first-order operators clearly annihilate g⁡(x)=exp⁡(r⁡(x))g(x)={\rm exp}(r(x)).

Holonomic functions in one variable are solutions to ordinary linear differential equations with rational function coefficients. Examples include algebraic functions, some elementary trigonometric functions, hypergeometric functions, Bessel functions, periods (as in Definition 2.13), and many more. But, not every nice function is holonomic. A necessary condition for a meromorphic function f⁡(x)f(x) to be holonomic is that it has only finitely many poles in the complex plane. The reason is that the singular locus of a holonomic DD-ideal is an algebraic variety in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. Thus, for n=1n=1 the singular locus must be a finite subset of ℂ\mathbb{C}.

For a concrete example, we note that f⁡(x)=1sin⁡(x)f(x)=\frac{1}{\sin(x)} is not holonomic. This shows that the class of holonomic functions is not closed under division, since sin(x)∈Sol(⟨∂2+1⟩)\,\sin(x)\in{\rm Sol}(\langle\partial^{2}+1\rangle). It is also not closed under composition of functions, since both 1x\frac{1}{x} and sin⁡(x)\sin(x) are holonomic. But, as a partial rescue, following [22, Theorem 2.7], we record the following positive result.

Proposition 2.3.

Let f⁡(x)f(x) be holonomic and g⁡(x)g(x) algebraic. Then f⁡(g⁡(x))f(g(x)) is holonomic.

Proof.

Let h≔f∘gh\coloneqq f\circ g. By the Chain Rule, all derivatives h(i)h^{(i)} can be expressed as linear combinations of f⁡(g),f′​(g),f′′​(g),…f(g),f^{\prime}(g),f^{\prime\prime}(g),\ldots with coefficients in ℂ⁡[g,g′,g′′,…]\mathbb{C}[g,g^{\prime},g^{\prime\prime},\ldots]. Since gg is algebraic, it fulfills some polynomial equation G⁡(g,x)=0G(g,x)=0. By deriving this polynomial equation, we can express each g(i)g^{(i)} as a rational function of xx and gg. We conclude that ℂ⁡[g,g′,…]⊂ℂ⁡(x,g)\mathbb{C}[g,g^{\prime},\ldots]\subset\mathbb{C}(x,g). Denote by WW the vector space spanned by f⁡(g),f′​(g),…f(g),f^{\prime}(g),\ldots over ℂ⁡(x,g)\mathbb{C}(x,g) and by VV the vector space spanned by f,f′,…f,f^{\prime},\ldots over ℂ⁡(x)\mathbb{C}(x). Since ff is holonomic, VV is finite-dimensional over ℂ⁡(x)\mathbb{C}(x). This implies that WW is finite-dimensional over ℂ⁡(g)\mathbb{C}(g), and therefore finite-dimensional over ℂ⁡(x,g)\mathbb{C}(x,g). Since gg is algebraic, ℂ⁡(x,g)\mathbb{C}(x,g) is finite-dimensional over ℂ⁡(x)\mathbb{C}(x). It follows that WW is a finite-dimensional vector space over ℂ⁡(x)\mathbb{C}(x), which means that h=f∘gh=f\circ g is holonomic. ∎

The term “holonomic function” was first proposed by D. Zeilberger [28] in the context of proving combinatorial identities. Building on Zeilberger’s work, among others, C. Koutschan [13] developed practical algorithms for manipulating holonomic functions. These are implemented in his Mathematica package HolonomicFunctions, as seen below.

Example 2.4.

Every algebraic function f⁡(x)f(x) is holonomic. Consider the function y=f⁡(x)y=f(x) that is defined by y4+x4+x​y100−1= 0y^{4}+x^{4}+\frac{xy}{100}-1\,=\,0. Its annihilator in DD can be computed as follows:

<< RISC‘HolonomicFunctions‘
q = y^4 + x^4 + x*y/100 - 1
ann = Annihilator[Root[q, y, 1], Der[x]]

This Mathematica code determines an operator PP of lowest order in AnnD⁡(f)\ann_{D}(f). We find

P=(2x4+1)2(25600000000x12−76800000000x8+76799999973x4−25600000000)∂3+6x3(2x4+1)(51200000000x12+76800000000x8−307199999946x4+179199999973)∂2+3x2(102400000000x16+204800000000x12+2892799999572x8−3507199999444x4+307199999953)∂−3​x​(102400000000​x16+204800000000​x12+1459199999796​x8−1049599999828​x4+51199999993).\small\begin{matrix}\!\!\!P\hskip 9.24994pt=\hskip 9.24994pt(2x^{4}+1)^{2}(25600000000x^{12}-76800000000x^{8}+76799999973x^{4}-25600000000)\,\partial^{3}\hskip 18.49988pt\hskip 9.24994pt\\ +6x^{3}(2x^{4}+1)(51200000000x^{12}+76800000000x^{8}-307199999946x^{4}+179199999973)\,\partial^{2}\\ +3x^{2}(102400000000x^{16}{+}204800000000x^{12}{+}2892799999572x^{8}{-}3507199999444x^{4}{+}307199999953)\,\partial\\ -3x(102400000000x^{16}+204800000000x^{12}+1459199999796x^{8}-1049599999828x^{4}+51199999993).\end{matrix}

This operator is an encoding of the algebraic function y=p⁡(x)y=p(x) as a holonomic function.

In computer algebra, one represents a real algebraic number as a root of a polynomial with coefficients in ℚ\mathbb{Q}. However, this minimal polynomial does not specify the number uniquely. For that, one also needs an isolating interval or sign conditions on derivatives. The situation is analogous for encoding a holonomic function ff in nn variables. We specify ff by a holonomic system of linear PDEs together with a list of initial conditions. The canonical holonomic representation is one example. Initial conditions such as (7) are designed to determine the function uniquely inside the linear space Sol⁡(I){\rm Sol}(I), where I⊆AnnD​(f)I\subseteq{\rm Ann}_{D}(f). For instance, in Example 2.4, we would need three initial conditions to specify the function p⁡(x)p(x) uniquely inside the 33-dimensional solution space to our operator PP. We could fix the values at three distinct points, or we could fix the value and the first two derivatives at one special point.

To be more precise, we generalize the canonical representation (7) as follows. A holonomic representation of a function ff is a holonomic DD-ideal I⊆AnnD⁡(f)I\subseteq\ann_{D}\left(f\right) together with a list of linear conditions that specify pp uniquely inside the finite-dimensional solution space of holomorphic solutions. The existence of this representation makes ff a holonomic function.

Before discussing more of the basic theory of holonomic functions, notably their remarkable closure properties, we first present an example that justifies the title of this lecture.

Example 2.5 (The area of a TV screen).

Let

q⁡(x,y)=x4+y4+1100​x​y−1.\displaystyle q(x,y)\,\,=\,\,x^{4}+y^{4}+\frac{1}{100}xy-1. (10)

We are interested in the semi-algebraic set S={(x,y)∈ℝ2∣q⁡(x,y)≤0}S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\mid q(x,y)\leq 0\}. This convex set is a slight modification of a set known in the optimization literature as “the TV screen”. Our aim is to compute the area of the semi-algebraic convex set SS as accurately as is possible.

One can get a rough idea of the area of SS by sampling. This is illustrated in Figure 1. From the equation we find that SS is contained in the square defined by −1.2≤x,y≤1.2-1.2\leq x,y\leq 1.2. We sampled 1000010000 points uniformly from that square, and for each sample we checked the sign of qq. Points inside SS are drawn in blue and points outside SS are drawn in pink. By multiplying the area (2.4)2=5.76(2.4)^{2}=5.76 of the square with the fraction of the number of blue points among the samples, we learn that the area of the TV screen is approximately 3.70773.7077.

We now compute the area more accurately using DD-modules. Let pr:S→ℝ\text{pr}\colon S\to\mathbb{R} be the projection on the xx-coordinate, and write v⁡(x)=ℓ⁡(pr−1​(x)∩S)v(x)=\ell\left({\rm pr}^{-1}(x)\cap S\right) for the length of a fiber. This function is holonomic and it satisfies the third-order differential operator in Example 2.4.

The map pr has two branch points x0<x1x_{0}<x_{1}. They are the real roots of the resultant

Resy​(q,∂q/∂y)=  25600000000​x12−76800000000​x8+76799999973​x4−25600000000.{\rm Res}_{y}(q,\partial{q}/\partial{y})\,\,=\,\,25600000000x^{12}-76800000000x^{8}+76799999973x^{4}-25600000000. (11)

These values can be written in radicals, but we take an accurate floating point representation:

x1=−x0= 1.000254465850258845478545766643566750080196276158976351763236​…x_{1}\,=\,-x_{0}\,=\,1.000254465850258845478545766643566750080196276158976351763236\ldots

The desired area equals vol⁡(S)=w⁡(x1){\rm vol}(S)=w(x_{1}), where ww is the holonomic function

w⁡(x)=∫x0xv⁡(t)​𝑑t.w(x)\,\,=\,\,\int_{x_{0}}^{x}v(t)dt.

One operator that annihilates ww is P∂P\partial, where P∈AnnD⁡(v)P\in\ann_{D}(v) is the third-order operator above. To get a holonomic representation of ww, we also need some initial conditions. Clearly, w⁡(x0)=0w(x_{0})=0. Further initial conditions on w′w^{\prime} are derived by evaluating vv at other points. By plugging values for xx into (10) and solving for yy, we find w′​(0)=2w^{\prime}(0)=2 and w′​(±1)=1/1003w^{\prime}(\pm 1)=1/\sqrt[3]{100}. Thus, we now have four linear constraints on our function ww, albeit at different points.

Our goal is to determine a unique function w∈Sol(P∂)w\in{\rm Sol}(P\partial) by incorporating these four initial conditions, and then to evaluate ww at x1x_{1}. To this end, we proceed as follows. Let xord∈ℝx_{\text{ord}}\in\mathbb{R} be any point at which P∂P\partial is not singular. Using the command local_basis_expansion that is built into the SAGE package ore_algebra, we compute a basis of local series solutions to P∂P\partial at the point xordx_{\text{ord}}. Since that point is non-singular, that basis has the following form:

sxord,0​(x)=1+O⁡((x−xord)4),sxord,1​(x)=(x−xord)+O⁡((x−xord)4),sxord,2​(x)=(x−xord)2+O⁡((x−xord)4),sxord,3​(x)=(x−xord)3+O⁡((x−xord)4).\begin{matrix}s_{x_{\text{ord}},0}(x)&=&1&+&O((x-x_{\text{ord}})^{4}),\\ s_{x_{\text{ord}},1}(x)&=&\!(x-x_{\text{ord}})\,&+&O((x-x_{\text{ord}})^{4}),\\ s_{x_{\text{ord}},2}(x)&=&(x-x_{\text{ord}})^{2}&+&O((x-x_{\text{ord}})^{4}),\\ s_{x_{\text{ord}},3}(x)&=&(x-x_{\text{ord}})^{3}&+&O((x-x_{\text{ord}})^{4}).\end{matrix} (12)

Indeed, by applying Proposition 1.18 locally at xordx_{\rm ord}, we get in(−1,1)(⟨P∂⟩)=⟨∂4⟩\ini_{(-1,1)}(\langle P\partial\rangle)=\langle\partial^{4}\rangle, and this DD-ideal has distraction J=⟨θ⁡(θ−1)​(θ−2)​(θ−3)⟩\,J=\langle\theta(\theta-1)(\theta-2)(\theta-3)\rangle\, with V⁡(J)={0,1,2,3}V(J)=\{0,1,2,3\}, by Theorem 1.20.

Locally at xordx_{\text{ord}}, our solution is given by a unique choice of four coefficients cxord,ic_{x_{\text{ord}},i}, namely

w⁡(x)=cxord,0⋅sxord,0​(x)+cxord,1⋅sxord,1​(x)+cxord,2⋅sxord,2​(x)+cxord,3⋅sxord,3​(x).w(x)\,\,=\,\,c_{x_{\rm ord},0}\cdot s_{x_{\text{ord}},0}(x)\,+\,c_{x_{\rm ord},1}\cdot s_{x_{\text{ord}},1}(x)\,+\,c_{x_{\rm ord},2}\cdot s_{x_{\text{ord}},2}(x)\,+\,c_{x_{\rm ord},3}\cdot s_{x_{\text{ord}},3}(x).

Let us point out that at a regular singular point xrsx_{\text{rs}}, complex powers of xx and log⁡(x)\log(x) can be involved in the local basis extension at xrsx_{\text{rs}}. We saw a series with log⁡(x)\log(x) in Example 1.25.

Any initial condition at that point determines a linear constraint on these coefficients. For instance, w′​(0)=2w^{\prime}(0)=2 implies c0,1=2c_{0,1}=2, and similarly for our initial conditions at −1,1-1,1 and x0x_{0}. One challenge we encounter here is that the initial conditions pertain to different points. To address this, we calculate transition matrices that relate the basis (12) of series solutions at one point to the basis of series solutions at another point. These are invertible 4×44\times 4 matrices. We compute them in SAGE with command op.numerical_transition_matrix.

With the method described above, we find the basis of series solutions at x1x_{1}, along with a system of four linear constraints on the four coefficients cx1,ic_{x_{1},i}. These constraints are derived from the initial conditions at 0,±10,\ \pm 1 and x0x_{0}, using the 4×44\times 4 transition matrices. By solving these linear equations, we compute the desired function value up to any desired precision:

w⁡(x1)= 3.708159944742162288348225561145865371243065819913934709438572​….w(x_{1})\,=\,3.708159944742162288348225561145865371243065819913934709438572....

In conclusion, this number is the area of the TV screen SS defined by the polynomial q⁡(x,y)q(x,y).

Let us now come back to properties of holonomic functions. Holonomic functions are very well-behaved with respect to many operations. They turn out to have remarkable closure properties. In the following, let f,gf,g be functions in nn variables x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}. In order to prove that a function is holonomic, we use one of the equivalent characterizations in Proposition 2.1.

Proposition 2.6.

If f,gf,g are holonomic functions, then both f+gf+g and f⋅gf\cdot g are holonomic.

Proof.

For each i∈{1,2,…,n}i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}, there exist non-zero operators Pi,Qi∈ℂ[x]⟨∂i⟩P_{i},Q_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[x]\langle\partial_{i}\rangle, such that Pi∙f=Qi∙g=0P_{i}\bullet f=Q_{i}\bullet g=0. Set ni=order⁡(Pi)n_{i}={\rm order}(P_{i}) and mi=order⁡(Qi)m_{i}={\rm order}(Q_{i}). The ℂ⁡(x)\mathbb{C}(x)-span of {∂ik∙f}k=0,…,ni\left\{\partial_{i}^{k}\bullet f\right\}_{k=0,\ldots,n_{i}} has dimension ≤ni\leq n_{i}. Similarly, the ℂ⁡(x)\mathbb{C}(x)-span of the set {∂ik∙g}k=0,…,mi\left\{\partial_{i}^{k}\bullet g\right\}_{k=0,\ldots,m_{i}} has dimension ≤mi\leq m_{i}.

Now consider ∂ik∙(f+g)=∂ik∙f+∂ik∙g\partial_{i}^{k}\bullet\left(f+g\right)=\partial_{i}^{k}\bullet f+\partial_{i}^{k}\bullet g. The ℂ⁡(x)\mathbb{C}(x)-span of {∂ik∙(f+g)}k=0,…,ni+mi\left\{\partial_{i}^{k}\bullet\left(f+g\right)\right\}_{k=0,\ldots,n_{i}+m_{i}} has dimension ≤ni+mi\leq n_{i}+m_{i}. Hence, there exists a non-zero operator Si∈ℂ[x]⟨∂i⟩S_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[x]\langle\partial_{i}\rangle, such that Si∙(f+g)=0S_{i}\bullet(f+g)=0. Since this holds for all indices ii, we conclude that the sum f+gf+g is holonomic.

A similar proof works for the product f⋅gf\cdot g. For each i∈{1,2,…,n}i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}, we now consider the set {∂ik∙(f⋅g)}k=0,1,…,ni​mi\left\{\partial_{i}^{k}\bullet\left(f\cdot g\right)\right\}_{k=0,1,\ldots,n_{i}m_{i}}. By applying Leibniz’ rule for taking derivatives of a product, we find that the mi​ni+1m_{i}n_{i}+1 generators are linear dependent over ℂ⁡(x)\mathbb{C}(x). Hence, there is a non-zero operator Ti∈ℂ[x]⟨∂i⟩T_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[x]\langle\partial_{i}\rangle such that Ti∙(f⋅g)=0T_{i}\bullet(f\cdot g)=0. We conclude that f⋅gf\cdot g is holonomic. ∎

Remark 2.7.

The proof above gives a linear algebra method for computing an annihilating DD-ideal II of finite holonomic rank for f+gf+g (resp. of f⋅gf\cdot g), starting from such DD-ideals for ff and gg. More refined methods for the same task can be found in [25, Section 3]. To get an ideal that is actually holonomic, it may be necessary to replace II by its Weyl closure W⁡(I)W(I).

The following example, similar to one in [28, Section 4.1], illustrates Proposition 2.6.

Example 2.8 (n=1n=1).

Consider the functions f⁡(x)=exp⁡(x)f(x)=\exp(x) and g⁡(x)=exp⁡(−x2)g(x)=\exp(-x^{2}). Their canonical holonomic representations are If=⟨∂−1⟩I_{f}=\langle\partial-1\rangle with f⁡(0)=1f(0)=1 and Ig=⟨∂+2x⟩I_{g}=\langle\partial+2x\rangle with g⁡(0)=1g(0)=1. We are interested in the function h=f+gh=f+g. Its first partial derivatives are

(h∂∙h∂2∙h)=(111−2​x14​x2−2)⋅(fg).\begin{pmatrix}h\\ \partial\bullet h\\ \partial^{2}\bullet h\end{pmatrix}\,\,\,=\,\,\,\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\ 1&-2x\\ 1&4x^{2}-2\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}f\\ g\end{pmatrix}.

By computing the left kernel of this 3×23\times 2-matrix, we find that h=f+gh=f+g is annihilated by

Ih=⟨(2x+1)∂2+(4x2−3)∂−4x2−2x+2⟩,withh(0)=2,h′(0)=1.I_{h}\,=\,\langle(2x+1)\partial^{2}+(4x^{2}-3)\partial-4x^{2}-2x+2\rangle,\hskip 10.00002pt\hbox{with}\,\,\,h(0)=2,\,h^{\prime}(0)=1.

For the product j=f⋅gj=f\cdot g we have j′=f′​g+f​g′=f⋅g+f⋅(−2​x​g)=(1−2​x)​j\,j^{\prime}\,=\,f^{\prime}g+fg^{\prime}=f\cdot g+f\cdot(-2xg)=(1-2x)j, so the canonical holonomic representation of jj is the DD-ideal Ij=⟨∂+2x−1⟩I_{j}=\langle\partial+2x-1\rangle with j⁡(0)=1j(0)=1.

Proposition 2.9.

Let ff be holonomic in nn variables and m<nm<n. Then the restriction of ff to the coordinate subspace {xm+1=…=xn=0}\{x_{m+1}=\ldots=x_{n}=0\} is a holonomic function in x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m}.

Proof.

For i∈{m+1,…,n}i\in\{m+1,\ldots,n\}, we consider the right ideal xi​Dnx_{i}D_{n} in the Weyl algebra DnD_{n}. This ideal is a left module over Dm=ℂ[x1,…,xm]⟨∂1,…,∂m⟩D_{m}=\mathbb{C}\left[x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}\right]\langle\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{m}\rangle. The sum of these ideals with AnnDn​(f){\rm Ann}_{D_{n}}(f) is hence a left DmD_{m}-module. Its intersection with DmD_{m} is called the restriction ideal:

(AnnDn⁡(f)+xm+1​Dn+⋯+xn​Dn)∩Dm.(\ann_{D_{n}}(f)+x_{m+1}D_{n}+\cdots+x_{n}D_{n})\,\,\cap\,\,D_{m}. (13)

By [19, Prop. 5.2.4], this DmD_{m}-ideal is holonomic and it annihilates f⁡(x1,…,xm,0,…,0)f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m},0,\ldots,0). ∎

Proposition 2.10.

The partial derivatives of a holonomic function are holonomic functions.

Proof.

Let ff be holonomic and Pi∈ℂ[x]⟨∂i⟩\{0}P_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[x]\langle\partial_{i}\rangle\backslash\{0\} with Pi∙f=0P_{i}\bullet f=0 for all ii. We can write PiP_{i} as Pi=Pi~∂i+ai(x)P_{i}=\widetilde{P_{i}}\partial_{i}+a_{i}(x), where ai∈ℂ⁡[x]a_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[x]. If ai=0a_{i}=0, then Pi~∙∂f∂xi=0\widetilde{P_{i}}\bullet\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}=0 and we are done. Assume ai≠0a_{i}\neq 0. Since both aia_{i} and ff are holonomic, by Proposition 2.6, there is a non-zero linear operator Qi∈ℂ[x]⟨∂i⟩Q_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[x]\langle\partial_{i}\rangle such that Qi∙(ai⋅f)=0Q_{i}\bullet(a_{i}\cdot f)=0. Then Qi​Pi~Q_{i}\widetilde{P_{i}} annihilates ∂f/∂xi\partial f/\partial x_{i}. ∎

Clearly, indefinite integrals of holonomic functions are holonomic functions. In order to prove the very same for the case of definite integrals, one has to work a little harder.

Proposition 2.11.

Let f:ℝn→ℂf\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{C} be a holonomic function. Then the definite integral

F⁡(x1,…,xn−1)=∫abf⁡(x1,…,xn−1,xn)​d​xnF(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1})\,\,=\,\,\int_{a}^{b}f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1},x_{n})dx_{n}

is a holonomic function in n−1n-1 variables, assuming the integral converges.

Proof.

It suffices to consider the case n=2n=2. By the elimination property in DD, there is a non-zero operator P(x1,∂1,∂2)∈DP(x_{1},\partial_{1},\partial_{2})\in D, independent of x2x_{2}, that annihilates ff. We rewrite

P(x1,∂1,∂2)=Q(x1,∂1)+∂2R(x1,∂1,∂2).P(x_{1},\partial_{1},\partial_{2})\,\,=\,\,Q(x_{1},\partial_{1})+\partial_{2}R(x_{1},\partial_{1},\partial_{2}).

Applying this operator to ff and taking the integral ∫ab\int_{a}^{b} on both sides of the equation yields

0=Q(x1,∂1)∙F(x1)+[R(x1,∂1,∂2)∙f]x2=ax2=b.\displaystyle 0\,\,=\,\,Q(x_{1},\partial_{1})\bullet F(x_{1})\,+\,\bigl[R(x_{1},\partial_{1},\partial_{2})\bullet f\bigr]_{x_{2}=a}^{x_{2}=b}. (14)

If the second summand in (14) is zero, then Q∈ℂ[x1]⟨∂1⟩Q\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1}]\langle\partial_{1}\rangle annihilates F⁡(x1)F(x_{1}) and we are done. Otherwise, that summand is a holonomic function in x1x_{1} by Propositions 2.9 and 2.10. Thus, there exists a non-zero operator Q~∈ℂ[x1]⟨∂1⟩\widetilde{Q}\in\mathbb{C}[x_{1}]\langle\partial_{1}\rangle that annihilates [R(x1,∂1,∂2)∙f]x2=ax2=b\left[R(x_{1},\partial_{1},\partial_{2})\bullet f\right]_{x_{2}=a}^{x_{2}=b}. It then follows that the operator Q~​Q\widetilde{Q}Q annihilates the function F⁡(x1)F(x_{1}).

Here is an alternative second proof. We can use the Heaviside function

H⁡(x)={0x<0,1x≥0,H(x)\,\,=\,\,\begin{cases}0&x<0,\\ 1&x\geq 0,\end{cases}

to rewrite the integral as follows:

F⁡(x1)=∫abf⁡(x1,x2)​d​x2=∫−∞∞H⁡(x2−a)​H​(b−x2)​f​(x1,x2)​d​x2.F(x_{1})\,\,=\,\,\int_{a}^{b}\!\!f(x_{1},x_{2})dx_{2}\,\,=\,\,\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\!H(x_{2}-a)H(b-x_{2})f(x_{1},x_{2})dx_{2}.

The distributional derivative of HH is given by the Dirac delta function δ\delta. Since x∙δ=0x\bullet\delta=0, the operator θ=x∂\theta=x\partial annihilates the Heaviside function, so H⁡(x)H(x) is a holonomic distribution. Adapting the above proof to the holonomic distribution H⁡(x2−a)​H​(b−x2)​f​(x1,x2)H(x_{2}-a)H(b-x_{2})f(x_{1},x_{2}), the second summand in (14) vanishes, since H⁡(x2−a)​H​(b−x2)​f​(x1,x2)H(x_{2}-a)H(b-x_{2})f(x_{1},x_{2}) is supported on [a,b][a,b]. ∎

Definition 2.12.

In the proof of Proposition 2.11, it is natural to consider the DmD_{m}-ideal

(AnnDn​(f)+∂m+1Dn+⋯+∂nDn)∩Dmfor m<n.\hskip 20.00003pt\bigl({\rm Ann}_{D_{n}}(f)\,\,+\,\,\partial_{m+1}D_{n}+\cdots+\partial_{n}D_{n}\bigr)\,\cap\,D_{m}\hskip 20.00003pt\text{for $m<n$.}

This is called the integration ideal with respect to the variables xm+1,…,xnx_{m+1},\ldots,x_{n}. The expression is dual to the restriction ideal (13) under the Fourier transform. This exchanges xix_{i} and ∂i\partial_{i}.

Equipped with our tools for manipulating holonomic functions, we now tackle the computation of volumes of compact semi-algebraic sets. We follow the work of P. Lairez, M. Mezzarobba and M. Safey El Din [15]. They compute this volume by deriving the Picard–Fuchs differential equation of the period of a certain rational integral. Here is the key definition.

Definition 2.13.

Let R⁡(t,x1,…,xn)R(t,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) be a rational function and consider the integral

∮R(t,x1,…,xn)dx1⋯dxn.\oint R(t,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})dx_{1}\cdots dx_{n}. (15)

Fix an open subset Ω\Omega of either ℝ\mathbb{R} or ℂ\mathbb{C}. An analytic function ϕ:Ω→ℂ\phi\colon\Omega\to\mathbb{C} is a period of the integral (15) if, for any s∈Ωs\in\Omega, there exists a neighborhood Ω′⊆Ω\Omega^{\prime}\subseteq\Omega of ss and an nn-cycle γ⊂ℂn\gamma\subset\mathbb{C}^{n} with the following property. For all t∈Ω′t\in\Omega^{\prime}, γ\gamma is disjoint from the poles of Rt≔R⁡(t,∙)R_{t}\coloneqq R(t,\bullet) and

ϕ(t)=∫γR(t,x1,…,xn)dx1⋯dxn.\phi(t)\,\,=\,\,\int_{\gamma}R(t,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})dx_{1}\cdots dx_{n}. (16)

If this holds, then there exists an operator P∈D\{0}P\in D\backslash\{0\} of the Fuchsian class annihilating ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t).

Let S={f≤0}⊂ℝnS=\left\{f\leq 0\right\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a compact basic semi-algebraic set, defined by a polynomial f∈ℚ⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in\mathbb{Q}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]. Let pr:ℝn→ℝ\text{pr}\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} denote the projection on the first coordinate. The set of branch points of pr is the following subset of the real line, which is assumed to be finite:

Σf={p∈ℝ∣∃x=(x2,…,xn)∈ℝn−1:f(p,x)=0and∂f∂xi(p,x)=0 for i=2,…,n}.\begin{matrix}\Sigma_{f}=\bigl\{p\in\mathbb{R}\mid\exists\,x=(x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}:f(p,x)=0\,\,\,\text{and}\,\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}(p,x)=0\,\text{ for }i=2,\ldots,n\bigr\}.\end{matrix}

The polynomial in the unknown pp that defines Σf\Sigma_{f} is obtained by eliminating x2,…,xnx_{2},\ldots,x_{n}. It can be represented as a multivariate resultant, generalizing the Sylvester resultant in (11).

Fix an open interval II in ℝ\mathbb{R} with I∩Σf=∅I\cap\Sigma_{f}=\emptyset. For any x1∈Ix_{1}\in I, the set Sx1≔pr−1​(x1)∩SS_{x_{1}}\coloneqq\text{pr}^{-1}(x_{1})\cap S\, is compact and semi-algebraic in (n−1)(n-1)-space. We are interested in its volume. By [15, Theorem 9], the function v:I→ℝ,x1↦voln−1​(Sx1)\,v\colon I\to\mathbb{R},\ x_{1}\mapsto\text{vol}_{n-1}\left(S_{x_{1}}\right)\, is a period of the rational integral

12​π​i∮x2f⁡(x1,x2,…,xn)∂f⁡(x1,x2,…,xn)∂x2dx2⋯dxn.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint\frac{x_{2}}{f(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})}\frac{\partial f(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n})}{\partial x_{2}}dx_{2}\cdots dx_{n}. (17)

Let e1<e2<⋯<eKe_{1}<e_{2}<\cdots<e_{K} be the branch points in Σf\Sigma_{f} and set e0=−∞e_{0}=-\infty and eK+1=∞e_{K+1}=\infty. This specifies the pairwise disjoint open intervals Ik=(ek,ek+1)I_{k}=\left(e_{k},e_{k+1}\right). They satisfy ℝ\Σf=⋃k=0KIk\,\mathbb{R}\backslash\Sigma_{f}=\bigcup_{k=0}^{K}I_{k}. Fix the holonomic functions wk​(t)=∫ektv⁡(x1)​d​x1\,w_{k}(t)=\int_{e_{k}}^{t}v(x_{1})dx_{1}. The volume of SS then is obtained as

voln​(S)=∫e1eKv⁡(x1)​d​x1=∑k=1K−1wk​(ek+1).\text{vol}_{n}\left(S\right)\,\,=\,\,\int_{e_{1}}^{e_{K}}\!\!v(x_{1})dx_{1}\,\,=\,\,\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}w_{k}\left(e_{k+1}\right).

How does one compute such an expression? As a period of the rational integral (17), the volume function vv is a holonomic function on each interval IkI_{k}. A key step is to compute a differential operator P∈D1P\in D_{1} that annihilates v∣Ikv\!\!\mid_{I_{k}} for all kk. With this, the product operator P∂P\partial annihilates the function wk​(x1)w_{k}(x_{1}) for k=1,…,K−1k=1,\ldots,K-1. By imposing sufficiently many initial conditions, we can reconstruct the functions wkw_{k} from the operator P∂P\partial uniquely. One initial condition that comes for free for each kk is wk​(ek)=0w_{k}(e_{k})=0.

The differential operator PP is known as the Picard–Fuchs equation of the period in question. The following software packages can be used to compute such Picard–Fuchs equations:

  • •

    HolonomicFunctions by C. Koutschan in Mathematica,

  • •

    ore_algebra by M. Kauers in SAGE,

  • •

    periods by P. Lairez in MAGMA,

  • •

    Ore_Algebra by F. Chyzak in Maple.

Our readers are encouraged to experiment with these programs.

We next discuss how one can actually compute the volume of our semi-algebraic set SS in practice. Starting from the defining polynomial ff, we compute the Picard–Fuchs operator P∈D1P\in D_{1} and we find sufficiently many compatible initial conditions. Thereafter, for each interval IkI_{k}, where k=1,…,K−1k=1,\ldots,K-1, we perform the following steps. We describe this for the ore_algebra package in SAGE, which we found to work well:

  1. (i)

    Using the command local_basis_expansion, compute a local basis of series solutions for the linear differential operator P∂P\partial at various points in [ek,ek+1)[e_{k},e_{k+1}).

  2. (ii)

    Using the command op.numerical_transition_matrix, numerically compute a transition matrix for the series solution basis from one point to another one.

  3. (iii)

    From the initial conditions construct linear relations between the coefficients in the local basis extensions. Using step (ii), transfer them to the branch point ek+1e_{k+1}.

  4. (iv)

    Plug in to the local basis extension at ek+1e_{k+1} and thus evaluate the volume of S∩pr−1​(Ik)S\cap\text{pr}^{-1}\left(I_{k}\right).

We now illustrate this recipe by computing the volume of a convex body in 33-space.

Example 2.14 (Quartic surface).

Fix the quartic polynomial

f⁡(x,y,z)=x4+y4+z4+x3​y20−x​y​z20−y​z100+z250−1,\displaystyle f(x,y,z)\,\,=\,\,x^{4}+y^{4}+z^{4}+\frac{x^{3}y}{20}-\frac{xyz}{20}-\frac{yz}{100}+\frac{z^{2}}{50}-1, (18)

and consider the set S={(x,y,z)∈ℝ3∣f⁡(x,y,z)≤0}\,S=\left\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\mid f(x,y,z)\leq 0\right\}. Our aim is to compute vol3​(S)\text{vol}_{3}\left(S\right).

As in Example 2.5 with the TV screen, we can get a rough idea of the volume of SS by sampling. This is illustrated in Figure 2. Our set SS is compact, convex, and contained in the cube defined by −1.05≤x,y,z≤1.05-1.05\leq x,y,z\leq 1.05. We sampled 1000010000 points uniformly from that cube. For each sample we checked the sign of f⁡(x,y,z)f(x,y,z). By multiplying the volume (2.1)3=9.261(2.1)^{3}=9.261 of the cube by the fraction of the number of gray points and the number of sampled points, SAGE found within few seconds that the volume of the quartic body SS is ≈6.4771\approx 6.4771. In order to obtain a higher precision, we now compute the volume of our set SS with help of DD-modules.

Let pr:ℝ3→ℝ\text{pr}\colon\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R} be the projection onto the xx-coordinate. Let v⁡(x)=vol2​(pr−1​(x)∩S)v(x)=\text{vol}_{2}\left({\rm pr}^{-1}(x)\cap S\right) denote the area of the fiber over any point xx in ℝ\mathbb{R}. We write e1<e2e_{1}<e_{2} for the two branch points of the map pr restricted to the quartic surface {f=0}\{f=0\}. They can be computed by help of resultants, for instance by the following steps in Singular with the library solve_lib [18]:

LIB "solve.lib";
ring r=0,(x,y,z),dp; setring r;
poly F=x^4+y^4+z^4+x^3*y*1/20-x*y*z*1/20-y*z*1/100+z^2*1/50-1;
def DFy=diff(F,y); def DFz=diff(F,z);
def resy=resultant(F,DFy,y); def resz=resultant(F,DFz,z);
ideal I=F,resy,resz;
def A=solve(I); setring A; SOL;

SOL is a list of the 3636 roots of the zero-dimensional ideal II. The first two of them are real and therefore are the branch points of pr. We obtain e1≈−1.0023512e_{1}\approx-1.0023512 and e2≈1.0024985e_{2}\approx 1.0024985.

By [15, Theorem 9], the area function v⁡(x)v(x) is a period of the rational integral

12​π​i​∮yf⁡(x,y,z)​∂f⁡(x,y,z)∂y​𝑑y​𝑑z.\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint\frac{y}{f(x,y,z)}\frac{\partial f(x,y,z)}{\partial y}dydz.

We set w⁡(t)=∫e1tv⁡(x)​𝑑xw(t)=\int_{e_{1}}^{t}v(x)dx. The desired 33-dimensional volume equals vol3​(S)=w⁡(e2)\text{vol}_{3}(S)=w(e_{2}).

Using Lairez’ implementation periods in MAGMA, we compute a differential operator PP of order eight that annihilates v⁡(x)v(x). Again, P∂P\partial then annihilates w⁡(x)w(x). One initial condition is w⁡(e1)=0w(e_{1})=0. We obtain eight further initial conditions w′​(x)=vol2​(Sx)w^{\prime}(x)=\text{vol}_{2}(S_{x}) for points x∈(e1,e2)x\in(e_{1},e_{2}) by running the same algorithm for the 22-dimensional semi-algebraic slices Sx=pr−1​(x)∩SS_{x}={\rm pr}^{-1}(x)\cap S. In other words, we make eight subroutine calls to an area measurement as in Example 2.5.

From these nine initial conditions we derive linear relations of the coefficients in the local basis expansion at e2e_{2}. These computations are run in SAGE as described in steps (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) above. We find the approximate volume of our convex body SS to be

≈6.4388324805728935447407338959699561889584208892351169762663289231288269155273887642162091495583989038294311376088934526903525560097601024171190804769405534826558114212766135380613959757935305271022089419155701521586470170874002194384529140686856227759541715097113399134734059617632892206072085516332397969163383760070738760107318247752061504714367250460900923409066377732273390396822296235214963623286613117557930687544148360721225681053481178760058264738867105810326818911578448323758536767168707442532146029753762594261578920477859.\begin{matrix}\approx 6.438832480572893544740733895969956188958420889235116976266328923128826\quad\\ 9155273887642162091495583989038294311376088934526903525560097601024171\\ 190804769405534826558114212766135380613959757935305271022089419155701\\ 52158647017087400219438452914068685622775954171509711339913473405961\\ 7632892206072085516332397969163383760070738760107318247752061504714\\ 367250460900923409066377732273390396822296235214963623286613117557\\ 930687544148360721225681053481178760058264738867105810326818911\\ 578448323758536767168707442532146029753762594261578920477859.\end{matrix}

This numerical value is guaranteed to be accurate up to 550550 digits.

3 Statistics

In this lecture, we explore the role of DD-modules in algebraic statistics. Our discussion centers around two themes. First, we study the Bernstein–Sato ideal of the likelihood function of a discrete statistical model. We present a case study that suggests a deep relationship between that ideal and maximum likelihood estimation. Thereafter, we turn to the holonomic gradient method (HGM) for continuous distributions. This method is the result of collaborations between statisticians and DD-module experts in Japan. We explain how HGM can be used for maximum likelihood estimation. This is implemented in an R package [27].

Let Dn=ℂ[x1,…,xn]⟨∂1,…,∂n⟩D_{n}=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]\langle\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}\rangle be the nnth Weyl algebra and adjoin one new formal variable ss that commutes with all xix_{i} and ∂j\partial_{j}. This defines the ring Dn​[s]D_{n}[s]. Fix a polynomial f∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in\mathbb{C}\left[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right] and consider the Dn​[s]D_{n}[s]-module ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn,fs,f−1,s]\mathbb{C}\left[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},f^{s},f^{-1},s\right]. Here the action of Dn​[s]D_{n}[s] on this module is given by the usual rules of calculus and arithmetic, in particular

∂i∙fs=s⋅∂f∂xi⋅f−1⋅fs=s⋅∂f∂xi⋅fs−1.\partial_{i}\bullet f^{s}\,\,=\,\,s\cdot\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}\cdot f^{-1}\cdot f^{s}\,\,=\,\,s\cdot\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}\cdot f^{s-1}.

The Bernstein–Sato polynomial of ff is the unique monic univariate polynomial bf∈ℂ⁡[s]b_{f}\in\mathbb{C}[s] of minimal degree such that P∙fs+1=bf⋅fsP\bullet f^{s+1}=b_{f}\cdot f^{s} for some P∈D⁡[s]P\in D[s]. The polynomial bfb_{f} was called the global bb-function in [19, Section 5.3], to which we refer for details. It is known that bfb_{f} is non-zero. M. Kashiwara [12] showed that all its roots are negative rational numbers. The Bernstein–Sato polynomial is computed as the generator of the following principal ideal:

⟨bf⟩=(AnnD⁡[s]​(fs)+⟨f⟩)∩ℂ⁡[s].\langle b_{f}\rangle\,\,=\,\,\left(\text{Ann}_{D[s]}\left(f^{s}\right)+\langle f\rangle\right)\,\cap\,\mathbb{C}[s].

Here, AnnD⁡[s]​(fs)={P∈D⁡[s]∣P∙fs=0}\,\text{Ann}_{D[s]}\left(f^{s}\right)=\left\{P\in D[s]\mid P\bullet f^{s}=0\right\}\, denotes the ss-parametric annihilator of fsf^{s}. A method for computing this D⁡[s]D[s]-ideal is found in [19, Algorithm 5.3.15].

We now pass to the case k≥2k\geq 2 of several polynomials f1,…,fk∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]f_{1},\ldots,f_{k}\in\mathbb{C}\left[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right]. Following [5] and the references therein, we define the Bernstein–Sato ideal of f=(f1,…,fk)f=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{k}) as

ℬ(f)=(AnnDn​[s1,…,sk](f1s1⋯fksk)+⟨f1⋯fk⟩)∩ℂ[s1,…,sk].\mathcal{B}\left(f\right)\,\,=\,\,\left(\,\ann_{D_{n}[s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}]}\left(f_{1}^{s_{1}}\cdots f_{k}^{s_{k}}\,\right)\,+\,\langle f_{1}\cdots f_{k}\rangle\right)\,\cap\,\,\mathbb{C}[s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}]. (19)

Here, s=(s1,…,sk)s=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}) and AnnDn​[s1,…,sk]​(fs)={P∈Dn​[s1,…,sk]∣P∙fs=0}\,\text{Ann}_{D_{n}[s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}]}\left(f^{s}\right)=\bigl\{P\in D_{n}[s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}]\mid P\bullet f^{s}=0\bigr\}\, denotes the ss-parametric annihilator of fs≔f1s1⋯fkskf^{s}\coloneqq f_{1}^{s_{1}}\cdots f_{k}^{s_{k}}. An implementation for performing the computation on the right hand side in (19) is available in the Singular library dmod_lib.

Note that the ideal ℬ⁡(f)\mathcal{B}(f) consists of all polynomials b∈ℂ⁡[s1,…,sk]b\in\mathbb{C}[s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}] that satisfy

b⋅∏i=1kfisi=P∙∏i=1kfisi+1for some P∈Dn​[s1,…,sk].\hskip 20.00003ptb\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{k}f_{i}^{s_{i}}\,\,=\,\,P\bullet\prod_{i=1}^{k}f_{i}^{s_{i}+1}\hskip 10.00002pt\hbox{for some $\,P\in D_{n}[s_{1},\ldots,s_{k}]$.}

For k=1k=1, the ideal ℬ⁡(f)\mathcal{B}(f) is generated by the Bernstein–Sato polynomial bfb_{f}. If k>1k>1, the Bernstein–Sato ideal is generally not principal. By [5, Theorem 1.5.1], the irreducible components of codimension one in the variety of ℬ⁡(f)\mathcal{B}\left(f\right) are hyperplanes of the special form

a1​s1+…+ak​sk+b=0 where ​a1,…,ak∈ℚ≥0​and​b∈ℚ>0.\displaystyle a_{1}s_{1}+\ldots+a_{k}s_{k}+b\,=0\,\hskip 10.00002pt\text{ where }\,\,a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\in\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}\,\,{\rm and}\,\,b\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}. (20)

This is an analogue of the fact that the roots of bf∈ℂ⁡[s]b_{f}\in\mathbb{C}[s] are negative rational numbers.

We are interested in studying the Bernstein–Sato ideals of parametric statistical models for discrete data. These models are families of probability distributions on kk states, where the probability of the iith state is given by a polynomial fif_{i}. The nn unknowns x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) represent the parameters of the models. A key feature of a statistical model is the identity

f1​(x)+f2​(x)+⋯+fk​(x)= 1,f_{1}(x)+f_{2}(x)+\cdots+f_{k}(x)\,=\,1, (21)

along with the reasonable semi-algebraic hypothesis ∃u∈ℝn​∀i∈{1,…,k}:fi​(u)>0\,\exists\,u\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\,\,\forall\,i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\,:\,f_{i}(u)>0. The coefficients of fif_{i} are usually rational numbers. We next present a familiar example.

Example 3.1 (Flipping a biased coin).

Let n=1n=1 and m=k−1m=k-1, so we can reindex from 00 to mm. Set fi​(x)=(mi)​xi​(1−x)m−i∈ℚ⁡[x]f_{i}(x)=\binom{m}{i}x^{i}(1-x)^{m-i}\in\mathbb{Q}[x] for i=0,…,mi=0,\ldots,m. The identity (21) holds by the Binomial Theorem. We also set fs≔f0s0f1s1⋯fmsmf^{s}\coloneqq f_{0}^{s_{0}}f_{1}^{s_{1}}\cdots f_{m}^{s_{m}}. The unknown xx represents the bias of the coin, a real number between 00 and 11. This is the probability that the coin comes up heads. Then fi​(x)f_{i}(x) is the probability of observing ii heads among mm independent coin tosses.

The ss-parametric annihilator AnnD⁡[s]​(fs)\,\text{Ann}_{D[s]}\left(f^{s}\right)\, is the D⁡[s]D[s]-ideal generated by

x(x−1)∂x−mx∑j=0msj+∑j=2m(j−1)sj.x(x-1)\partial_{x}-mx\sum_{j=0}^{m}s_{j}+\sum_{j=2}^{m}(j-1)s_{j}.

This is the result of a computation for small values of mm. The Bernstein–Sato ideal ℬ⁡(f)⊂ℚ⁡[s0,…,sm]\mathcal{B}\left(f\right)\subset\mathbb{Q}[s_{0},\ldots,s_{m}] is obtained by adding f0f1⋯fmf_{0}f_{1}\cdots f_{m} to this ideal and then eliminating xx and ∂\partial. We find that ℬ⁡(f)\mathcal{B}\left(f\right) is the principal ideal generated by the following product of linear forms:

∏j=1(m+12)(s1+2​s2+⋯+m​sm+j)⋅∏k=1(m+12)(m​s0+(m−1)​s1+⋯+sm−1+k).\prod_{j=1}^{\binom{m+1}{2}}\left(s_{1}+2s_{2}+\cdots+ms_{m}+j\right)\cdot\prod_{k=1}^{\binom{m+1}{2}}\left(ms_{0}+(m-1)s_{1}+\cdots+s_{m-1}+k\right). (22)

One sees that all factors are linear forms with positive coefficients, as predicated in (20). Note that we can recover these linear factors in a combinatorial way from the following table:

f0f_{0} f1f_{1} … fm−1f_{m-1} fmf_{m} ∑\sum
xx\hskip 10.00002pt 0 1 … m−1m-1 mm (m+12)\binom{m+1}{2}
1−x1-x\, mm m−1m-1 … 1 0 (m+12)\binom{m+1}{2}

Each column means that fif_{i} is a monomial in xx and 1−x1-x with the indicated exponents.

The validity of the formula (22) can be derived from the results on hyperplane arrangements in [4, Section 6]. The point is that for n=1n=1 parameter, each fif_{i} is a product of linear forms, by the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra. Hence, f1f2⋯fkf_{1}f_{2}\cdots f_{k} defines an arrangement in ℝ1\mathbb{R}^{1}. The rows of the table indicate the multiplicity of each hyperplane in the product.

In the context of statistics, the sis_{i} represent nonnegative integers which summarize an independent and identically distributed sample. Namely, sis_{i} is the number of observations of the iith outcome. The sum s1+s2+⋯+sks_{1}+s_{2}+\cdots+s_{k} is the sample size of the experiment. The function fs=f1s1f2s2⋯fksk\,f^{s}\,=\,f_{1}^{s_{1}}f_{2}^{s_{2}}\cdots f_{k}^{s_{k}} is the likelihood function of the model with respect to the data. We think of ss as parameters, so we are interested in the situation when the model is fixed and the data varies. The vector ss of counts ranges over ℕk\mathbb{N}^{k}, or even over ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k} or ℂk\mathbb{C}^{k}, and we treat its coordinates sis_{i} as unknowns. The role of the likelihood function fsf^{s} in data analysis can be summarized by referring to the two historic strands in the field of statistics:

  • •

    Frequentist statistics: Compute argmax⁡(fs)\,{\rm argmax}(f^{s}), i.e., solve an optimization problem.

  • •

    Bayesian statistics: Compute ∫γfs​𝑑x\,\int_{\gamma}f^{s}dx, i.e., evaluate a certain definite integral.

We refer to Sullivant’s book [24, Chapter 5] for a discussion of these two perspectives. The integration problem is reminiscent of the volume computation in the previous lecture. Let us now discuss the optimization problem. This is known as maximum likelihood estimates (MLE). The aim is to maximize fsf^{s} over a suitable open subset of parameters xx in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. To address this problem algebraically, one studies the map that associates to ss the critical points. This map is an algebraic function. The number of its branches is known as the maximum likelihood degree (ML degree); see [11] and [24, Chapter 7]. Models of special interest are those where the ML degree is one. This means that the MLE is given by a rational function. Such models were studied recently in [7]. The following two examples have this property.

Example 3.2 (Example 3.1 revisited).

Consider the model where a biased coin is flipped mm times. The likelihood function fsf^{s} has its unique critical point at

x^=1m⋅m⋅s0+(m−1)⋅s1+⋯+1⋅sm−1+0⋅sms0+s1+s2+⋯+sm.\hat{x}\hskip 10.00002pt=\hskip 10.00002pt\frac{1}{m}\cdot\frac{m\cdot s_{0}+(m-1)\cdot s_{1}+\cdots+1\cdot s_{m-1}+0\cdot s_{m}}{s_{0}+s_{1}+s_{2}+\cdots+s_{m}}.

The probability estimates fi​(x^)\,f_{i}(\hat{x})\, are alternating products of linear forms in the counts s0,s1,…,sms_{0},s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}. The linear forms appearing in the numerators are precisely those in (22).

Example 3.3.

We examine the model that serves as the running example in [7]. It concerns the following simple experiment: Flip a biased coin. If it shows heads, then flip it again. Here k=3,m=2k=3,m=2 and n=1n=1. The model is given algebraically by f0=x2\,f_{0}=x^{2}, f1=x⁡(1−x)f_{1}=x(1-x), and f2=1−xf_{2}=1-x. These three polynomials in ℚ⁡[x]\mathbb{Q}[x] sum to 11. The likelihood function equals

fs=f0s0​f1s1​f2s2=x2​s0+s1⋅(1−x)s1+s2.f^{s}\,\,=\,\,f_{0}^{s_{0}}f_{1}^{s_{1}}f_{2}^{s_{2}}\,\,=\,\,x^{2s_{0}+s_{1}}\cdot(1-x)^{s_{1}+s_{2}}.

This is annihilated by the following first-order operator:

P=(x2−x)∂−(2s0+s1+s2)x+s1+s2∈D[s0,s1,s2].P\,\,=\,\,(x^{2}-x)\partial\,-\,(2s_{0}+s_{1}+s_{2})x\,+s_{1}+s_{2}\,\,\in\,\,D[s_{0},s_{1},s_{2}].

We consider the D⁡[s]D[s]-ideal generated by PP and x⁡(1−x)x(1-x), and we eliminate xx and ∂\partial to find

ℬ⁡(f)=⟨∏k=13(2​s0+s1+k)⋅∏l=12(s1+s2+l)⟩.\mathcal{B}\left(f\right)\hskip 10.00002pt=\hskip 10.00002pt\biggl\langle\,\prod_{k=1}^{3}\left(2s_{0}+s_{1}+k\right)\cdot\prod_{l=1}^{2}\left(s_{1}+s_{2}+l\right)\,\biggr\rangle.

Thus, the Bernstein–Sato ideal is principal and generated by a product of linear forms (20). As before, we recover the linear factors appearing in ℬ⁡(f)\mathcal{B}(f) from a table of multiplicities:

f0f_{0} f1f_{1} f2f_{2} ∑\sum
xx 22 11 00 33
1−x1-x 0 1 1 22

This mirrors the formula in [7, Example 2] for the maximum likelihood estimate:

x^=2​s0+s12​s0+2​s1+s2,1−x^=s1+s22​s0+2​s1+s2.\hat{x}\,=\,\frac{2s_{0}+s_{1}}{2s_{0}+2s_{1}+s_{2}}\,,\hskip 20.00003pt1-\hat{x}\,=\,\frac{s_{1}+s_{2}}{2s_{0}+2s_{1}+s_{2}}.

Just like in Example 3.1, the numerators are precisely the linear factors in ℬ⁡(f)\mathcal{B}(f).

Our discussion suggests that there is a deeper connection between DD-module theory and likelihood geometry [11]. This deserves to be explored. Further, it would be interesting to study the Bayesian integrals ∫γfs\int_{\gamma}f^{s} using the DD-module methods from the previous lecture.

We now come to the Holonomic Gradient Method (HGM). Consider the problem of maximum likelihood estimation in statistics, but now for continuous distributions rather than discrete ones. Our aim is to explain the benefit gained from DD-module theory. Indeed, many functions of relevance in statistics are holonomic. A key idea is to compute and represent the gradient of such a function from its canonical holonomic representation.

The statistical aim of MLE is to find parameters such that an observed outcome is most probable [24, Chapter 7].
