This can be formulated as an optimization problem, namely to maximize the likelihood function. For discrete models, this function has the form fsf^{s}, as seen above. In what follows we consider the likelihood function for continuous models.

Our goal is to find a local maximum of a holonomic function using a variant of gradient descent. For the sake of efficiency, our computations are carried out in the rational Weyl algebra R=ℂ(x)⟨∂⟩R=\mathbb{C}(x)\langle\partial\rangle. See [19, Section 1.4] for the theory of Gröbner bases in RR. Unless otherwise stated, we use the graded reverse lexicographical order ≺\prec. For n=2n=2, this gives

1≺∂2≺∂1≺∂22≺∂1∂2≺∂12≺⋯.1\prec\partial_{2}\prec\partial_{1}\prec\partial_{2}^{2}\prec\partial_{1}\partial_{2}\prec\partial_{1}^{2}\prec\cdots.

Let f⁡(x1,…,xn)f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) be a real-valued holonomic function and II a DD-ideal with finite holonomic rank such that I∙f=0I\bullet f=0. Thus, R/IR/I is finite-dimensional over ℂ\mathbb{C}. In our application, ff will be the likelihood function of a statistical model. Let rank⁡(I)=m∈ℕ>0\rank(I)=m\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}. We write S={s1,…,sm}S=\left\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}\right\}, with s1=1s_{1}=1, for the set of standard monomials for a Gröbner basis of R​IRI in RR. By Proposition 2.10, the mm entries of the following vector are holonomic functions

F=(s1∙f,s2∙f,…,sm∙f)T.F\,\,=\,\,\left(s_{1}\bullet f,s_{2}\bullet f,\ldots,s_{m}\bullet f\right)^{T}.

Note that the first entry of FF is the given function ff. In symbols, (F)1=f(F)_{1}=f. Since II has holonomic rank mm, there exist unique matrices P1,…,Pn∈ℂ​(x1,…,xn)m×mP_{1},\ldots,P_{n}\in\mathbb{C}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})^{m\times m} such that

∂i∙F=Pi⋅Ffor i=1,…,n.\displaystyle\hskip 20.00003pt\partial_{i}\bullet F=P_{i}\cdot F\hskip 20.00003pt\text{for }i=1,\ldots,n. (23)

The system of linear partial differential equations (23) is called the Pfaffian system of ff. Note that it depends on the specific RR-ideal II and on the chosen term order. The matrices PiP_{i} can be computed as follows. We apply the division algorithm modulo our Gröbner basis to the operators ∂isj,\partial_{i}s_{j}, for i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\ldots,n\} and j∈{1,…,m}j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}. The resulting normal form equals

aj​1(i)​(x)​s1+aj​2(i)​(x)​s2+⋯+aj​m(i)​(x)​sm,a^{(i)}_{j1}(x)s_{1}\,+\,a^{(i)}_{j2}(x)s_{2}\,+\,\cdots\,+\,a^{(i)}_{jm}(x)s_{m},

where the coefficients aj​k(i)a^{(i)}_{jk} are certain rational functions in x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}. This means that the operator ∂isj−∑k=1maj​k(i)​(x)​sk\,\partial_{i}s_{j}-\sum_{k=1}^{m}a^{(i)}_{jk}(x)s_{k}\, is in the RR-ideal II. From this one sees that the coefficient aj​k(i)​(x)a^{(i)}_{jk}(x) is the entry of the m×mm\times m matrix PiP_{i} in row jj and column kk.

We have now reached the following important conclusion. Suppose xx is replaced by a point uu in ℚn\mathbb{Q}^{n}. Here uu might be a highly accurate floating point representation of a point in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. The numerical evaluation of the gradient of ff at uu reduces to multiplying the vector F⁡(u)∈ℚmF(u)\in\mathbb{Q}^{m} by matrices Pi​(u)P_{i}(u) with explicit rational entries. A tacit assumption made here is that uu lies in the complement of the singular locus of the Pfaffian system (23) that encodes ff.

Example 3.4 (n=1n=1).

Let ff be a holonomic function annihilated by the DD-ideal I=⟨x∂3−(x+1)∂+1⟩\,I\,=\,\langle\,x\partial^{3}-(x+1)\partial+1\,\rangle. The generator by itself is a Gröbner basis for R​IRI. The set of standard monomials equals S={1,∂,∂2}S=\{1,\partial,\partial^{2}\}, and this is a ℂ\mathbb{C}-basis of R/R​IR/RI. From II we see that

∂3∙f=x+1x∂∙f−1x⋅f.\partial^{3}\bullet f\,\,=\,\,\frac{x+1}{x}\partial\bullet f\,-\,\frac{1}{x}\cdot f.

Let F=(f,∂∙f,∂2∙f)TF=(f,\partial\bullet f,\partial^{2}\bullet f)^{T}. This yields the following Pfaffian system for our function ff:

∂∙F=P⋅FwhereP=(010001−1xx+1x0).\displaystyle\partial\bullet F=P\cdot F\hskip 10.00002pt{\rm where}\hskip 10.00002ptP=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\\ -\frac{1}{x}&\frac{x+1}{x}&0\end{pmatrix}.

Using the notation familiar from calculus, for any non-zero real number uu, this means

(f′​(u)f′′​(u)f′′′​(u))=(010001−1uu+1u0)⋅(f⁡(u)f′​(u)f′′​(u)).\begin{pmatrix}f^{\prime}(u)\\ f^{\prime\prime}(u)\\ f^{\prime\prime\prime}(u)\end{pmatrix}\hskip 10.00002pt=\hskip 10.00002pt\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\\ -\frac{1}{u}&\frac{u+1}{u}&0\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}f(u)\\ f^{\prime}(u)\\ f^{\prime\prime}(u)\end{pmatrix}.

This matrix-vector formula is useful for applying numerical algorithms as uu ranges over ℝ\mathbb{R}.

Given a holonomic function ff, represented by a holonomic DD-ideal, we are interested in the following two questions. The first of these was already discussed in the previous lecture.

  1. (1)

    How to evaluate ff at a point with the help of the knowledge of II?

  2. (2)

    How to find local minima of ff with the help of the knowledge of II?

We first describe how to evaluate the holonomic function ff at a point x~\tilde{x} by a first order approximation. Assume we are able to numerically evaluate ff at some particular point x(0)x^{(0)}, depending on the precise situation. Choose a path x(0)→x(1)→⋯→x(K)=x~x^{(0)}\to x^{(1)}\to\cdots\to x^{(K)}=\tilde{x}, with x(k+1)x^{(k+1)} sufficiently close to x(k)x^{(k)} for all k=0,…,K−1k=0,\ldots,K-1 and such that the path does not cross the singular locus of the Pfaffian system of ff. The following algorithm is referred to as the

Holonomic Gradient Method (HGM).

  1. 1.

    Compute a Gröbner basis of R​IRI in the rational Weyl algebra RR.

  2. 2.

    Identify the set of standard monomials SS and compute the Pfaffian system (23) of ff.

  3. 3.

    Numerically evaluate FF at one point x(0)x^{(0)} and denote the result by F¯\bar{F}. Set k=0k=0.

  4. 4.

    Approximate the value of the vector FF at x(k+1)x^{(k+1)} by its first-order Taylor polynomial:

    F⁡(x(k+1))\displaystyle F(x^{(k+1)}) ≈F(x(k))+∑i=1n(xi(k+1)−xi(k))⋅(∂i∙F)(x(k))\displaystyle\,\,\approx\,\,F(x^{(k)})\,+\,\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i}^{(k+1)}-x_{i}^{(k)})\cdot(\partial_{i}\bullet F)(x^{(k)})
    =F⁡(x(k))+∑i=1n(xi(k+1)−xi(k))⋅Pi​(x(k))⋅F¯.\displaystyle\,\,=\,\,F(x^{(k)})\,+\,\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_{i}^{(k+1)}-x_{i}^{(k)}\right)\cdot P_{i}\left(x^{(k)}\right)\cdot\bar{F}.

    Denote the result by F¯\bar{F}.

  5. 5.

    Increase the value of kk by 11. If k<Kk<K, return to step 4. Otherwise stop.

Observe that steps 1 to 3 need to be carried out only once for (f,I)(f,I). The output of this algorithm is a vector F¯\bar{F} that approximates F⁡(x~)F(\tilde{x}). The first coordinate of F⁡(x~)F(\tilde{x}) is the desired scalar f⁡(x~)f(\tilde{x}). Hence the first coordinate of F¯\bar{F} is our numerical approximation of that scalar.

Remark 3.5.

To turn the HGM into a practical algorithm, it is essential to incorporate some knowledge from numerical analysis. For instance, there is a lot of freedom in choosing the numerical approximation method in step 4. Nakayama et al. [17] use the Runge–Kutta method of fourth order. Another common variant is to use a second order Taylor approximation. Here one computes the Hessian of ff also by means of the Pfaffian system of ff.

Remark 3.6.

The Gröbner basis computation in step 1 may not terminate, but sometimes a partial Gröbner basis for R​IRI suffices to certify holonomicity. From this one gets a finite superset SS of the unknown set of true standard monomials. The set SS spans R/R​IR/RI, but it may not be linearly independent. In that case, one can still compute a Pfaffian system, but the PiP_{i} are not necessarily unique anymore. This relaxation might work well in practice.

We are now endowed with all necessary tools for finding a local minimum of the holonomic function ff. As before, ff is encoded by an annihilating DD-ideal II with finite holonomic rank.

Holonomic Gradient Descent (HGD).

  1. 1.

    Compute a Gröbner basis of R​IRI in the rational Weyl algebra RR.

  2. 2.

    Identify the set of standard monomials SS and compute the Pfaffian system (23) of ff.

  3. 3.

    Numerically evaluate F⁡(x(0))F(x^{(0)}) at some starting point x(0)x^{(0)} and put k=0k=0. Denote this value by F¯\bar{F}. The evaluation method is chosen to be adapted to the problem.

  4. 4.

    For i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, numerically evaluate the first coordinate of Pi​(x(k))​F¯\,P_{i}(x^{(k)})\bar{F}. Let G¯\bar{G} be the vector of these nn numbers. This G¯\bar{G} approximates the gradient ∇f\nabla f at x(k)x^{(k)}, since

    ∂i∙f=(∂i∙F)1=(Pi⋅F)1.\,\partial_{i}\bullet f\,\,=\,\,\left(\partial_{i}\bullet F\right)_{1}\,\,=\,\,(P_{i}\cdot F)_{1}.
  5. 5.

    If a termination condition of the iteration is satisfied, stop. Otherwise go to step 6.

  6. 6.

    Put x(k+1)=x(k)−hk​G¯x^{(k+1)}=x^{(k)}-h_{k}\bar{G}, where hkh_{k} is an appropriately chosen step length.

  7. 7.

    Numerically evaluate FF at x(k+1)x^{(k+1)} by step 4 of the HGM and set this value to F¯\bar{F}. Increase the value of the index kk by one and return to step 4 above.

The algorithm returns a point x(k)x^{(k)} along with the value of ff at that point. This output is a numerical approximation of a local minimum of the holonomic function ff. Again, one should be aware that this algorithm works only within connected components contained in the complement of the singular locus of the Pfaffian system of ff.

In order to develop a practical implementation, and to assess the quality of the method, one needs some expertise from numerical analysis. The choices one makes can make a huge difference. For instance, consider the choice of the step size hkh_{k}. This is a well-studied subject in numerical optimization, and there are various standard recipes for carrying out gradient descent. In current applications to data science, stochastic versions of gradient descent play a major role, and it would be very nice to connect DD-modules to these developments.

The applicability of HGD arises from the fact that many distributions that are used in practice are given by holonomic functions. One example is the cumulative distribution function of the largest eigenvalue of a Wishart matrix, cf. [9]. Another relevant holonomic function is the likelihood function of sampling matrices in SO​(3)\text{SO}(3). In what follows we present in detail an example that stood at the beginning of the development of HGM and HGD.

Example 3.7 (The Fisher–Bingham distribution [17]).

Let 𝕊n​(r)={x∈ℝn+1∣∥x∥=r}\,\mathbb{S}^{n}(r)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\mid\lVert x\rVert=r\right\}\, denote the nn-sphere of radius rr. Let x∈ℝ(n+1)×(n+1)x\in\mathbb{R}^{(n+1)\times(n+1)} be a symmetric matrix and y∈ℝn+1y\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1} a row vector. Let |d​t|\lvert dt\rvert denote the standard measure on 𝕊n​(r)\mathbb{S}^{n}(r). The Fisher–Bingham integral is

F⁡(x,y,r)=∫𝕊n​(r)exp⁡(tT​x​t+y​t)​|𝑑t|.F(x,y,r)\hskip 10.00002pt=\hskip 10.00002pt\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n}(r)}\!\!\exp\left(t^{T}xt+yt\right)|dt|.

This is a function in (n+12)+(n+1)+1\binom{n+1}{2}+(n+1)+1 unknowns, since xk​l=xl​kx_{kl}=x_{lk}. It is shown in [17, Theorem 1] that the function F⁡(x,y,r)F(x,y,r) is holonomic. More precisely, the following operators annihilate the Fisher–Bingham integral and generate a DD-ideal of finite holonomic rank:

∑i=1n+1∂xi​i−r2,r∂r−2∑i≤jxi​j∂xi​j−∑iyi∂yi−n,∂xi​j−∂yi∂yjfori≤j,xi​j∂xi​i+2(xj​i−xi​i)∂xi​j−xi​j∂xj​j+∑k≠i,j(xj​k∂xi​k−xi​k∂xj​k)+yj∂yi−yi∂yjfori<j.\begin{matrix}\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\partial_{x_{ii}}-r^{2}\,,\quad r\partial_{r}-2\sum_{i\leq j}x_{ij}\partial_{x_{ij}}-\sum_{i}y_{i}\partial_{y_{i}}-n\,,\quad\partial_{x_{ij}}-\partial_{y_{i}}\partial_{y_{j}}\,\,\,{\rm for}\,\,\,i\leq j,\vskip 3.0pt plus 1.0pt minus 1.0pt\\ x_{ij}\partial_{x_{ii}}+2(x_{ji}-x_{ii})\partial_{x_{ij}}-x_{ij}\partial_{x_{jj}}+\sum_{k\neq i,j}(x_{jk}\partial_{x_{ik}}-x_{ik}\partial_{x_{jk}})+y_{j}\partial_{y_{i}}-y_{i}\partial_{y_{j}}\,\,\,{\rm for}\,\,\,i<j.\\ \end{matrix}

For a proof, see [17, Theorems 2,3]. For n=1,2n=1,2, these operators generate a holonomic DD-ideal, see [17, Proposition 1]. We now define the Fisher–Bingham distribution on the unit sphere 𝕊n​(1)\mathbb{S}^{n}(1). This depends on the parameters x,yx,y and has the probability density function

p⁡(t∣x,y)=F​(x,y,1)−1⋅exp⁡(tT​x​t+y​t).p(t\!\mid\!x,y)\,\,\,=\,\,\,F(x,y,1)^{-1}\cdot\exp(t^{T}xt+yt).

In other words, the Fisher–Bingham distribution plays the role of the Gaussian distribution on the sphere, and the Fisher–Bingham integral F⁡(x,y,1)F(x,y,1) is its normalizing constant.

We now explain the statistical inference problem to be solved. Let {t⁡(1),…,t⁡(N)}\{t(1),\ldots,t(N)\} be an independent and identically distributed sample of size NN on the unit sphere 𝕊n​(1)\mathbb{S}^{n}(1). The statistical aim is to estimate the parameters x=(xi​j)x=(x_{ij}) and y=(yi)y=(y_{i}) from the given sample. The standard method to do so is MLE. We seek to maximize the likelihood function

(x,y)↦∏ν=1Np⁡(t⁡(ν)∣x,y).(x,y)\,\,\mapsto\,\,\prod_{\nu=1}^{N}p(t(\nu)\!\mid\!x,y).

For the Fisher–Bingham model, this task is equivalent to minimizing the function

F(x,y,1)⋅exp(−∑1≤i≤j≤n+1Si​jxi​j−∑1≤i≤n+1Siyi)\displaystyle F(x,y,1)\cdot\exp\left(-\sum_{1\leq i\leq j\leq{n+1}}S_{ij}x_{ij}-\sum_{1\leq i\leq{n+1}}S_{i}y_{i}\right) (24)

Here the SiS_{i} and Si​jS_{ij} are real constants that are easily computed from the sample points t⁡(i)t(i). Namely, they are the coordinates of the sample mean and the sample covariance matrix:

Si=N−1​∑ν=1Nti​(ν)andSi​j=N−1​∑ν=1Nti​(ν)​tj​(ν).S_{i}\,=\,N^{-1}\sum_{\nu=1}^{N}t_{i}(\nu)\hskip 10.00002pt{\rm and}\hskip 10.00002ptS_{ij}\,=\,N^{-1}\sum_{\nu=1}^{N}t_{i}(\nu)t_{j}(\nu).

The function (24) is a product of two holonomic functions. Hence, it is a holonomic function in the unknowns x=(xi​j)x=(x_{ij}) and y=(yi)y=(y_{i}). Furthermore, since our model is an exponential family, the logarithm of (24) is a convex function. This means that a local minimum is already a global one. Our task is therefore to find a local minimum of (24) using HGD.

The authors of [17] present two specific data sets and they demonstrate the use of HGD for this input. The data and some code in the computer algebra system Risa/Asir are provided at the website http://www.math.kobe-u.ac.jp/OpenXM/Math/Fisher-Bingham/.

One of the data sets is the following “astronomical data”. Here n=2n=2 and

S1=−0.0063,S2=−0.0054,S3=−0.0762,S11=0.3199,S12=0.0292,S13=0.0707,S22=0.3605,S23=0.0462,S33=0.3276.\begin{matrix}&S_{1}=-0.0063,\ S_{2}=-0.0054,\ S_{3}=-0.0762,\vskip 3.0pt plus 1.0pt minus 1.0pt\\ &S_{11}=0.3199,\ S_{12}=0.0292,\ S_{13}=0.0707,\ S_{22}=0.3605,\ S_{23}=0.0462,\ S_{33}=0.3276.\\ \end{matrix}

The start point is found by minimizing with a quadratic approximation of F⁡(x,y,1)F(x,y,1), and the step size was set at 0.050.05. Running the HGD revealed the minimum objective function value ≈11.6857\approx 11.6857, and the maximum likelihood parameters were found to be

x=(−0.1610.3377/21.1104/20.3377/20.25380.6424/21.1104/20.6424/2−0.0928),y=(−0.019,−0.0162,−0.2286).\displaystyle x\,=\,\begin{pmatrix}-0.161&0.3377/2&1.1104/2\\ 0.3377/2&0.2538&0.6424/2\\ 1.1104/2&0.6424/2&-0.0928\end{pmatrix},\hskip 10.00002pty\,=\,(-0.019,-0.0162,-0.2286).

We reproduced this result, but this did take some effort.

In conclusion, we have argued that holonomic functions arise in many contexts, notably in geometry and statistics. The manipulation of these functions can be done by algorithms from the theory of DD-modules. Many implementations already exist, and they are available in a wide range of computer algebra systems. While the further development of the symbolic computation tools is important, a significant new opportunity lies in advancing the connection to numerical algebraic geometry. Efficient numerical methods for DD-modules and holonomic functions have a clear potential for future impact in scientific computing and data science. These lectures offered a very first glimpse at the underlying mathematics.

Problems

In this section, we offer some ideas for hands-on activities. These were discussed in an afternoon session during the Berlin school. The items range from easy exercises to challenging questions that suggest research projects. We leave it to our readers to decide which is which.

  1. 1.

    Let MM be a DD-module which is finite-dimensional as a ℂ\mathbb{C}-vector space. Show that M=0M=0. Hint: Can the commutator of two n×nn\times n-matrices be the identity matrix?

  2. 2.

    Find bases of solutions for the following three second-order linear differential equations:

    x​f′′+f′=0andg′′=4​x2​gandx2​h′′−3​x​h′+4​h=0.xf^{\prime\prime}+f^{\prime}=0\hskip 10.00002pt{\rm and}\hskip 10.00002ptg^{\prime\prime}=4x^{2}g\hskip 10.00002pt{\rm and}\hskip 10.00002ptx^{2}h^{\prime\prime}-3xh^{\prime}+4h=0.
  3. 3.

    For each of the following three functions u,v,wu,v,w in one variable xx, find a linear ordinary differential equation with polynomial coefficients that is satisfied by that function:

    u⁡(x)=x3/5⋅log​(x)2,v⁡(x)=sin​(x)5,w⁡(x)=(1+x4)⋅exp⁡(x).u(x)\,=\,x^{3/5}\cdot{\rm log}(x)^{2},\hskip 10.00002ptv(x)\,=\,{\rm sin}(x)^{5},\hskip 10.00002ptw(x)\,=\,(1+x^{4})\cdot{\rm exp}(x).
  4. 4.

    A ℂ\mathbb{C}-basis of the Weyl algebra D=ℂ[x1,…,xn]⟨∂1,…,∂n⟩D=\mathbb{C}\left[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\right]\langle\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}\rangle consists of the normal monomials xa∂bx^{a}\partial^{b}, where a,b∈ℕna,b\in\mathbb{N}^{n}. Find the formula for the operator ∂bxa\partial^{b}x^{a} in that basis.

  5. 5.

    Let n=3n=3 and consider the DD-ideal I=⟨∂14,∂24,∂34,∂1∂22∂33,∂12∂23∂3,∂13∂2∂32⟩\,I=\langle\partial_{1}^{4},\partial_{2}^{4},\partial_{3}^{4},\partial_{1}\partial_{2}^{2}\partial_{3}^{3},\partial_{1}^{2}\partial_{2}^{3}\partial_{3},\partial_{1}^{3}\partial_{2}\partial_{3}^{2}\rangle. Compute the distraction I~\widetilde{I} in ℂ⁡[θ1,θ2,θ3]\mathbb{C}[\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3}] and find a ℂ\mathbb{C}-basis for the vector space Sol⁡(I)=Sol⁡(I~)\,{\rm Sol}(I)={\rm Sol}(\widetilde{I}).

  6. 6.

    Find a canonical holonomic representation for the bivariate function

    f⁡(x,y)=ex⋅y⋅sin​y1+y2.f(x,y)\hskip 10.00002pt=\hskip 10.00002pte^{x\cdot y}\cdot{\rm sin}\frac{y}{1+y^{2}}.
  7. 7.

    Using the integration ideal as in Definition 2.12, find an operator in D1D_{1} that annihilates

    F⁡(x)=∫0+∞f⁡(x,y)​𝑑y,where f is the function in Problem 6.\hskip 20.00003ptF(x)\hskip 10.00002pt=\hskip 10.00002pt\int_{0}^{+\infty}\!\!f(x,y)dy,\hskip 20.00003pt\text{where $f$ is the function in Problem 6.}
  8. 8.

    Construct a rational function rr by taking the ratio of your two favorite polynomials in two variables. Compute I=AnnD⁡(r)I=\ann_{D}(r) and determine the singular locus Sing⁡(I)⊂ℂ2{\rm Sing}(I)\subset\mathbb{C}^{2}.

  9. 9.

    Let f⁡(x)f(x) be a holonomic function in one variable. Show that its reciprocal 1/f⁡(x)1/f(x) is holonomic if and only if the logarithmic derivative f′​(x)/f​(x)f^{\prime}(x)/f(x) is an algebraic function.

  10. 10.

    For those who like sheaves: Why is a vector bundle together with a flat connection a module over the sheaf 𝒟\mathcal{D}? Actually, what are these objects over the projective line ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}?

  11. 11.

    For those who like toric geometry: Pick your favorite projective toric manifold and write the presentation ideal (Stanley–Reisner plus linear forms) of its Chow ring in ℂ[∂1,…,∂n]\mathbb{C}[\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}] and also in ℂ⁡[θ1,…,θn]\mathbb{C}[\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n}]. Determine the solution spaces in both cases.

  12. 12.

    For those who like the Hodge theory of matroids: Pick your favorite matroid and write the presentation ideal (Stanley–Reisner plus linear forms) of its Chow ring in ℂ[∂1,…,∂n]\mathbb{C}[\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}] and also in ℂ⁡[θ1,…,θn]\mathbb{C}[\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{n}]. Determine the solution spaces in both cases.

    Stafford’s Theorem states that every DD-ideal can be generated by two elements. Let n=4n=4 and identify two differential operators that generate the DD-ideal ⟨∂1,∂2,∂3,∂4⟩\langle\partial_{1},\partial_{2},\partial_{3},\partial_{4}\rangle.     Let n=9n=9, where xi​j,∂i​jx_{ij},\partial_{ij} are entries of 3×33\times 3 matrices. Let PP be the prime ideal in ℂ⁡[xi​j]\mathbb{C}[x_{ij}] that defines the group SO⁡(3){\rm SO}(3) in ℂ3×3\mathbb{C}^{3\times 3}. Let II be the DD-ideal generated by PP and

    {∑k=13(xk​i∂k​j−xk​j∂k​i):  1≤i<j≤3}.\biggl\{\,\sum_{k=1}^{3}(x_{ki}\partial_{kj}-x_{kj}\partial_{ki})\,\,:\,\,1\leq i<j\leq 3\,\biggr\}.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
